title: Tibetan delegation meets UNHRC special representative, presents six demands
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Aug. 14:A Tibetan delegation, accompanied by two family members of late Tibetan independence activist Lobga Rangzen, met with United Nations Human Rights Council Special Representative Anne Siyota at the United Nations on Wednesday, urging the international rights body to take more decisive action over the deteriorating human rights situation in Tibet. The delegation, led by former 13th and 14th Tibetan Youth Congress (TYC) Centrex President and former Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile member Tsewang Rigzin, held discussions with Siyota for nearly an hour. Speaking toPhayulfollowing the meeting, he said the delegation submitted six demands that addressed what it described as “continuing violations”of Tibetan rights and the erosion of Tibet’s cultural and national identity. The delegation’s first demand was for the United Nations to implement its earlier resolutions on Tibet adopted in 1959, 1961 and 1965. These resolutions had raised concerns over violations of the fundamental rights and freedoms of the Tibetan people and called for an end to policies undermining their rights, including their right to self-determination. The delegation also urged the UN to dispatch an independent fact-finding mission to Tibet and recognise Tibet as an independent country, with sovereignty vested in the Tibetan people. A significant portion of the discussion focused on China’s education policies in Tibet, particularly the expansion of state-run residential boarding schools for Tibetan children. Rigzen toldPhayulthat the delegation called on the UN to exert pressure on Beijing to dismantle the boarding-school system, which they allege is designed to accelerate the assimilation of Tibetan children into Chinese society by distancing them from their families, language, and cultural traditions. The delegation further urged the United Nations to publicly oppose China’s recently implementedLaw on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, calling for the legislation to be withdrawn immediately. The sixth demand centred on what Rigzen described as the need for the United Nations to show greater solidarity with and sympathy for the Tibetan people. As part of this appeal, the delegation asked a UN representative to visit the site outside the UN Headquarters in New York where the late martyr carried out self-immolation on July 2, 2026. The Tibetan activist later died from his injuries. The delegation also called on the UN to acknowledge and honour the thousands of Tibetan men and women who, according to the delegation, have sacrificed their lives for the Tibetan cause over the years. He said the six demands were ultimately aimed at pressing the UN to move beyond expressions of concern and take more tangible steps on the Tibet issue. These, he said, should include enforcing its earlier resolutions, facilitating an independent investigation into conditions in Tibet, challenging policies viewed as threatening Tibetan identity, and giving greater recognition to the rights and grievances of the Tibetan people. title: New visuals show intensified demolition at Larung Gar, monk detained after protest
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Aug. 14:Newly obtained photographs and video footage by Dharamshala-based media outlets showed demolition work is continuing at Larung Gar Buddhist Institute in Sertar County, eastern Tibet, offering a rare visual glimpse into the latest phase of a campaign that has already affected more than 1,000 monastic residences. The newly surfaced footage appears to show monastic residences being evicted as Chinese authorities proceed with the latest round of demolitions at one of the world’s largest centres of Tibetan Buddhist learning. According to reports, on August 9, a monk staged a protest against the demolition by displaying a large portrait of the 10th Panchen Lama from the window of a residence marked for destruction. The portrait reportedly remained suspended for a considerable period, apparently as a symbolic rejection of the authorities’ actions. The monk was subsequently detained, according to reports, and his whereabouts remain unknown. The reported detention of the monk who displayed the portrait of the 10th Panchen Lama adds another dimension to the latest demolition campaign. His current whereabouts remain unknown, highlighting concerns over the treatment of monks who publicly object to measures affecting Tibetan religious institutions. The latest demolition drive comes against the backdrop of intensified restrictions at Larung Gar, which has been subjected to successive government campaigns over the past two decades. Chinese authorities carried out major demolitions in 2001, 2016, and 2019, citing overcrowding and the lack of legally required construction permits. The latest phase began on July 13, 2026, with more than 1,000 residences reportedly slated for demolition. Founded in 1980 by the late Tibetan Buddhist master Khenpo Jigme Phuntsok, Larung Gar was established in the aftermath of the Cultural Revolution as a centre for the revival of Buddhist learning and meditation. It subsequently developed into a prominent institution for the study and practice of Tibetan Buddhism, as well as a major centre for Tibetan language and cultural education, drawing thousands of Tibetan and Han Chinese practitioners. Its rapid growth, however, brought the institute under sustained scrutiny from Chinese authorities. In 2001, authorities launched the first major demolition campaign at Larung Gar, destroying thousands of residential structures and reducing the institute’s population by roughly half. Despite continuing restrictions, the community gradually expanded again. A far larger campaign followed in 2016 and 2017 after a directive from the central government. Nearly 5,000 residences were reportedly demolished, while thousands of monks and nuns were expelled from the institute. The measures prompted international concern. In February 2017, six United Nations human rights experts warned that the actions at Larung Gar appeared to constitute “concerted attacks on tangible and intangible cultural heritage” and raised concerns over violations of the cultural rights of both present and future generations. The pressure on Larung Gar has extended beyond the physical dismantling of residences. Since 2019, Chinese authorities have progressively tightened restrictions on the enrolment and participation of Han Chinese Buddhists at the institute. In 2021, authorities reportedly introduced measures separating Chinese practitioners from Tibetan residents, further altering the demographic composition and functioning of the academy. The latest demolitions therefore represent another chapter in a prolonged process of restructuring and curbing the religious community. Access to Larung Gar has also become increasingly restricted, making independent reporting from inside the sprawling complex difficult. The emergence of the latest photographs and video footage consequently provides an uncommon glimpse into the continuing changes taking place within the institute. title: Two Tibetans honoured with ‘Rangeland Restoration Awards’ for grassroots conservation and pastoralism
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 6:Two Tibetans, Trachung Palzang from Ngawa (Ch. Sichuan) and Hashu Karma Choshas from Yushu (Ch. Qinghai), have been honoured with theRangeland Restoration Awards 2026for their contributions to grassland restoration, pastoral livelihoods, ecological conservation, and the preservation of Tibetan nomadic culture. The awards, organised under the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists (IYRP) 2026, declared by the United Nations General Assembly, recognised 20 practitioners from 90 entries across 26 countries. The awards were jointly organised by the IYRP Global Alliance and the South Asia Regional Alliance, honouring individuals whose work contributes to the restoration, sustainable management and protection of rangelands, while strengthening the pastoral communities that depend on them. Trachung Palzang, from Gascha Village in Maixi Township, Dzoge County, Ngawa Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, is described as a community-based grassland restoration practitioner and a member of a traditional herding family. According to his award profile, Palzang returned home in 2010 to address grassland degradation and help safeguard pastoral culture. He subsequently combined traditional pastoral knowledge with modern ecological approaches and, in 2013, founded a grassland restoration cooperative, alongside a herder photography group that has engaged hundreds of pastoralists in ecological restoration and cultural preservation. His work has reportedly contributed to the restoration of approximately 14,000 mu, or 933 hectares, of degraded alpine grasslands and peat wetlands through community-led approaches. Palzang has also promoted summer enclosure and winter grazing, as well as adaptive grazing practices aimed at improving the sustainability of rangeland management. His initiatives have benefited about 280 pastoral households, representing more than 1,200 people, while engaging over 1,000 herders. His conservation efforts have also focused on biodiversity, with his award profile noting improved habitat conditions supporting 98,000 sheep units and more than 230 wildlife species. Beyond ecological restoration, Palzang has worked to strengthen indigenous knowledge and pastoral culture, including through the establishment of a herder photography group and a community conservation model that has reportedly been replicated by more than 10 organisations. Hashu Karma Choshas, from Jialo Grassland in Drido County, Yushu Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, is recognised as a nomadic educator, cultural heritage bearer, and grassland guardian. A member of a pastoral community, he founded the Polar Nomadic School, an initiative that integrates ecological education with traditional nomadic knowledge. The school has reportedly reached more than 5,000 students, herders, and teachers. His work extends beyond environmental conservation to the preservation of Tibetan nomadic heritage. He is recognised as a county-level intangible cultural heritage bearer for Shengto-style black-tent craftsmanship and has worked to revive and preserve the traditional craft. He has also founded the Yushu Third Pole Ecological Nomadic Culture Protection and Development Research Service Center, linking cultural preservation with community-based ecological conservation. His award profile credits him with protecting and restoring more than 5,000 mu, approximately 333 hectares, of alpine grassland through rotational grazing. The landscape lies near the source of Drichu (Yangtze River) and the headwaters of the Neqü River and supports approximately 300 yaks and 100 Tibetan sheep within a traditional pastoral setting. He has additionally worked with local communities to conserve water sources, particularly the headwaters of the Neqü River, while promoting ecological education and traditional pastoral knowledge. The recognition comes at a time when Tibetan pastoral communities face mounting pressures from environmental degradation and policies by the Chinese government that have disrupted their traditional relationship with the land. Large-scale infrastructure under the pretext of development projects—including roads, airports, dams, mining operations, reservoirs, solar power facilities, and national parks—have transformed vast stretches of traditional grazing grounds, while other interventions have further restricted access to pasturelands. Under the Chinese government’s ecological and animal husbandry policies, nomads have increasingly been restricted from seasonal grazing and, in many areas, compelled to settle in fixed locations. Grasslands have been fenced off, converted for other uses, or subjected to large-scale mining and other development activities, contributing to ecological degradation and the fragmentation of traditional pastoral landscapes. These changes have had consequences beyond the environment. The displacement of nomadic communities and restrictions on traditional pastoral practices have disrupted longstanding livelihoods, weakened community networks, and placed pressure on the transmission of Tibetan language, culture, and pastoral knowledge. title: Flash floods, debris damage roads, pastures at sacred Mount Amnye Machen
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 7:Flash floods and extensive debris flows struck Mount Amnye Machen in Machen County, Golog Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, Amdo (Ch. Qinghai), on the evening of August 5, damaging roads and bridges and burying large stretches of pastureland, following what a source in exile described as a glacier collapse on the mountain. The source in exile who wished to remain anonymous for security reasons toldPhayulthat the glacier collapse triggered torrents of water, mud, and rock that swept through an uninhabited section of the mountain. No human or livestock casualties have been reported, but the debris flow has covered substantial areas of surrounding pasture under thick layers of mud and debris. The source said the scale of the flooding and debris flow has significantly altered parts of the landscape and warned that unstable terrain could continue to pose risks to pilgrims travelling along the mountain’s traditional circumambulation route. Chinese authorities, however, attributed the damage to heavy rainfall and mudslides. An official notice dated August 25 stated that rural roads and bridges had been damaged and warned of geological hazards and risks to traffic safety. Authorities subsequently prohibited vehicles and pedestrians from entering the affected areas, citing the need to safeguard lives and property. The notice did not mention a glacier collapse. The disaster has also disrupted a major pilgrimage season at Mount Amnye Machen, one of Tibet’s four principal sacred mountains. The mountain holds particular religious significance during the Year of the Horse, when large numbers of Tibetan pilgrims traditionally undertake the circumambulation around its sacred perimeter. Following the flooding, authorities suspended pilgrim travel along the affected routes. Despite indications from local officials that repairs would be completed swiftly, the roads remained closed as of September 6. Many pilgrims have consequently been stranded in the Tamchok Gongkha area of Yaekhok village, waiting for the route to reopen so they can resume and complete their pilgrimage. Warnings circulating on Tibetan social media have urged pilgrims to exercise caution, citing the continuing possibility of avalanches, landslides and other hazards along sections of the circuit. The flooding has also renewed longstanding concerns among local Tibetans over the environmental impact of mining in the Amnye Machen range. According to the exile source, discussions circulating on Tibetan social media have linked the recent glacier collapse and flooding to decades of mining activity around the mountain, although the connection has not been independently established. Local residents have reportedly observed a marked retreat of glaciers in recent years, exposing ground and animal trails that were previously covered by thick layers of ice. The changes have fuelled concerns about the mountain’s increasingly fragile environment and the potential risks facing communities and pilgrims who depend on the surrounding landscape. Mining operations in the Amnye Machen range reportedly began around 1993, with operations transferred to Qinghai West Copper Co., Ltd. in 1997. Over the following decades, intensive mineral extraction, particularly for copper, has drawn repeated criticism from local residents and Tibetan environmental advocates over its alleged impact on the ecology of the sacred mountain range. Concerns have also been raised over alleged pollution of the Guchu River. Local accounts have claimed that untreated industrial wastewater was discharged directly into the river, rendering the water unsuitable for consumption by nomadic communities and contributing to livestock deaths. Residents have repeatedly appealed to local authorities over the alleged environmental damage associated with mining. On August 21, 2017, they reportedly submitted a petition to Chinese central government departments calling for the mining project to be halted. According to local accounts, however, their appeals have not resulted in a substantive halt to mining activities. The latest disaster has consequently intensified concerns over the deteriorating ecological conditions around Mount Amnye Machen, where glacial retreat, extreme weather, mining activity and the seasonal influx of pilgrims converge in a landscape considered sacred by Tibetans. title: China restrict Tibetan volunteers, relief efforts in flood-hit Kyirong
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 4:Chinese authorities have imposed stringent restrictions on movement into flood-hit Kyirong region in occupied Tibet, preventing Tibetans from other parts of the region from travelling to the disaster zone to provide relief and express solidarity with affected communities, according to an exile-based source who spoke to Phayul on condition of anonymity for safety reasons. The source said the Chinese government has adopted an unusually restrictive approach to relief efforts in Kyirong, where severe flooding has affected areas along the Tibet-Nepal border. “Many Tibetans want to travel to Kyirong to help the affected people, but they are not being allowed to enter the area,” the source told Phayul, adding that the restrictions appear particularly stringent given the region’s proximity to Nepal. According to a government notice issued following the floods, entry into the affected border area is restricted to officially designated relief personnel. Civilians and personal vehicles are prohibited from entering the disaster zone, while travel from Saga, Tingri and Nyalam Counties into Kyirong has been explicitly barred for civilians. Authorities have warned that those who violate the restrictions could face severe legal consequences. The source contrasted the restrictions with the response to the devastating January 2025 Dingri earthquake, during which some Tibetan-led relief and assistance efforts were reportedly permitted. “This time, the restrictions are much stricter. During the 2025 Dingri earthquake, some Tibetans were able to provide assistance, but in Kyirong they are not allowing such efforts at all,” the source said. The source stated that the heightened controls may be linked to Kyirong’s strategic location on the Nepal border, where authorities are particularly sensitive to the movement of people and information. Meanwhile, Chinese state controlled propaganda mouthpiece have released carefully curated photographs and videos showing government-led rescue and relief operations in the affected areas. The imagery focuses on state-organised emergency responses and relief personnel, while independent access to the disaster zone remains heavily restricted. In the aftermath of the catastrophic floods and mudslides that swept parts of the Tibet-Nepal border on August 26, Chinese authorities reported 31 deaths and 531 people missing in occupied Tibet as of September 4. The figures, however, remain impossible to independently verify, as journalists, international humanitarian organisations, and other independent observers continue to be denied access to the disaster-affected areas. The absence of independent access has compounded concerns over the transparency of the official casualty figures and left substantial gaps in public knowledge about the scale of the devastation. For families searching for missing relatives, the restrictions have created an acute information vacuum, prolonging an agonising wait for credible and timely confirmation of their loved ones’ fate and whereabouts. Chinese authorities said that, by noon on September 2, they had received 876 calls reporting people dead or missing—448 from within China and 428 from overseas. The volume of calls highlights the magnitude of the uncertainty surrounding the disaster and the growing demand from families for reliable information from authorities. title: Dalai Lama returns to Dharamshala after more than two-month sojourn in Ladakh
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 4:The Tibetan spiritual leader His Holiness the Dalai Lama returned to Dharamshala on Friday after spending more than two months in Leh, Ladakh, bringing to a close an extended summer sojourn marked by religious teachings, public audiences, and engagements with people from across the Himalayan region. The nonagenarian leader was warmly welcomed by thousands of Tibetans and local Indian residents who lined the streets of Dharamshala as his convoy made its way to his residence. The spiritual leader had been in Ladakh from June 28 to September 4, following medical treatment for his left knee in Delhi. His annual summer visits to Ladakh have become a longstanding practice, allowing him to escape Dharamshala’s intense monsoon season while continuing his religious and public engagements in the Himalayan region. During his stay, the Dalai Lama held public audiences in Leh for 49 days, receiving a total of 21,572 people. He also attended a Long-Life Prayer offering at the Kalachakra Teaching Ground, a gathering that reflected the region’s distinctive interfaith character. The prayer ceremony was jointly organised by the Ladakh Buddhist Association, Ladakh Gonpa Association, the Muslim communities represented by Anjuman Imamia and Anjuman Moin-ul-Islam, and the Christian community of Ladakh. The Dalai Lama’s return to Dharamshala follows a period of heightened attention to his health and mobility. He underwent surgery on his left knee in June this year in Delhi, following a successful right knee replacement performed in June 2025 at Hospital for Special Surgery (HSS) in New York, one of the world’s leading orthopaedic centres. After his 2025 procedure, the Tibetan spiritual leader spent a period recovering in Syracuse, New York, where he underwent extensive physical therapy before returning to Dharamshala. Despite persistent mobility challenges, the Dalai Lama has maintained a demanding public schedule in recent years, continuing to conduct religious teachings, grant audiences, and participate in official and community engagements. During large public gatherings, he has occasionally relied on aides and a golf cart to cover longer distances between his residence and the Tsuglagkhang, the Main Tibetan Temple, where he regularly conducts teachings and public ceremonies. title: Real Madrid deletes Nepal-Tibet flood post after Chinese backlash
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 3:Spanish football powerhouse Real Madrid has deleted a social media post referring to victims of the devastating Tibet-Nepal floods, days after the club came under intense criticism from Chinese state media and online users for using the word “Tibet” rather than Beijing’s sinicised term “Xizang.” The post, which had appeared on Real Madrid’s official social media platforms on August 30, featured a photograph of players observing a minute’s silence at the Santiago Bernabéu for victims of the catastrophic floods and landslides that struck communities on both sides of the Tibet-Nepal border on August 26. The accompanying message referred to those affected in “Nepal and Tibet.” The post was removed on September 3, following mounting criticism in China. Although Real Madrid has not publicly stated that the deletion was made in response to Chinese pressure, its removal came after Chinese state-affiliated media and online users repeatedly demanded that the club retract or amend the wording. The Global Times, a Chinese Communist Party mouthpiece, urged Real Madrid to replace “Tibet” with “China’s Xizang”, arguing that the club’s humanitarian gesture had been overshadowed by what it described as politically inaccurate wording. The newspaper stressed that “Xizang is an inalienable part of China” and said placing it alongside the sovereign nation of Nepal ran counter to the one-China principle. Chinese social media users also piled pressure on the club, calling for the post to be deleted and for Real Madrid to issue an apology. The criticism was accompanied by a pointed reminder of the club’s commercial stakes in the Chinese market. The Global Times noted that Real Madrid commands a sizeable following in China and has cultivated long-term commercial interests across Asia, warning that the club’s public communications are therefore expected to meet a higher threshold of sensitivity when addressing territorial issues. The deletion marks a striking turn in a controversy that began with what was ostensibly a humanitarian gesture. A football club’s expression of solidarity with victims of a natural disaster has instead become entangled in one of China’s most sensitive political fault lines: the terminology used to describe Tibet. Beijing officially refers to Tibet as “Xizang” and has increasingly sought to promote that terminology in international discourse. The Chinese government regards Tibet as an integral part of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) and strongly objects to language that, in its view, treats Tibet as a separate political entity. Real Madrid’s decision to remove the post, without publicly explaining the reason, has therefore raised questions over the extent to which China’s political sensitivities can shape the public communications of major international brands seeking to maintain relations with Chinese audiences. The episode also illustrates how the language surrounding Tibet has become a contested arena far beyond diplomatic and political circles. Even a condolence message from one of the world’s most prominent football clubs has been subjected to scrutiny over whether it conforms to Beijing’s preferred nomenclature. The dispute comes as the humanitarian toll from the August 26 disaster continues to mount. A massive ice-and-rock avalanche near the Tibet-Nepal border unleashed catastrophic flash floods, devastating communities and infrastructure and leaving thousands dead or missing. As of September 3, Nepal had recorded at least 1,252 deaths, while more than 4,200 people remained missing. Across the border in occupied Tibet, Chinese authorities have officially acknowledged 16 deaths and hundreds of people missing, even as Kyirong—one of the hardest-hit areas—bore the brunt of the devastating floods. The stark disparity in reported casualties has fuelled concerns over the transparency and completeness of information coming from the Tibetan side of the border. title: Tibetan, Chinese pro-democracy advocates adopt joint declaration at Dharamshala forum
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 3:A three-day forum bringing together Tibetan and Chinese scholars, policy experts, and human rights activists concluded in Dharamshala on Wednesday with a joint call for nonviolence, democratic reform, and sustained dialogue as pathways towards a peaceful resolution of the Tibet-China conflict. The “Democratic China and Future of Tibet Forum”, organised by the Tibetan Community Development Fund (TCDF) in collaboration with the Central Tibetan Administration’s official think tank, Tibet Policy Institute (TPI), brought together 29 participants from India, the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Germany, the Netherlands, Australia, Japan, Taiwan, and Southern Mongolia. Convened to foster candid exchanges on democracy, human rights, and Tibet’s political future, the forum sought to bridge perspectives between Tibetans and Chinese pro-democracy activists and explore avenues for greater cooperation between the Tibetan and Chinese democratic movements. The forum opened on August 31 with a keynote address by CTA President Penpa Tsering, who spoke on Sino-Tibetan relations, the Middle Way Approach, the reincarnation of the 14th Dalai Lama, and the importance of cooperation between Tibetans and Chinese. The discussions culminated in five declarations covering nonviolence, a shared democratic future, Tibetan democracy and history, the Dalai Lama’s reincarnation, and the legal and human-rights implications of China’sLaw on the Promotion of Ethnic Unity and Progress. The first declaration established nonviolence as a common guiding principle for addressing the Tibet-China conflict. Participants drew on the longstanding advocacy of the 14th Dalai Lama and Chinese democracy advocate Liu Xiaobo, emphasising peaceful resistance, dialogue, and pragmatic engagement as alternatives to confrontation. The second declaration called for a shared vision of a democratic future, urging closer interaction between Tibetans in exile and Chinese democracy organisations and individuals. Participants also highlighted the value of sharing the Tibetan exile community’s experience of democratic governance as part of broader efforts towards democratisation in China. Discussions under the third declaration focused on Tibet’s history, Tibetan-Chinese exchanges, Tibetan democracy, and the Middle Way Approach. Participants said greater understanding of Tibetan perspectives among Chinese audiences, alongside deeper Tibetan engagement with China’s democracy movement, could help build trust and create space for meaningful dialogue. The declaration also called for greater efforts to explain the Middle Way Approach to Chinese people. The policy, advocated by the Tibetan leadership in exile, seeks genuine autonomy for Tibetans within the framework of the Chinese Constitution rather than outright independence. The fourth declaration addressed the reincarnation of the 14th Dalai Lama, rejecting any role for the Chinese government in the process. Participants stated that the authority to determine the Dalai Lama’s succession rests with the Dalai Lama and the Dalai Lama’s private office, Gaden Phodrang Trust, in accordance with Tibetan Buddhist traditions. The fifth declaration raised concerns over China’s so-called “Law on the Promotion of Ethnic Unity and Progress,” calling for its immediate repeal. Participants argued that the legislation could have far-reaching consequences for the linguistic, cultural, religious, and national identities of Tibetans, Uyghurs, Southern Mongolians, and other ethnic communities. The participants said the forum marked a step towards establishing a sustained platform for Tibetan-Chinese academic and policy engagement, with continued communication and cooperation envisioned as a means of building mutual understanding and strengthening nonviolent approaches to the long-running conflict. title: Book honouring Lobga Rangzen’s legacy launched in Dharamshala
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 2:Marking two months since the passing of Tibetan independence activist Lobga Rangzen, a collection of 77 essays and prose pieces written by Tibetans in the aftermath of his self-immolation was launched on Wednesday at the Tibetan Settlement Office (TSO) hall in Dharamshala. The volume brings together writings that appeared across social media platforms following Lobga Rangzen’s death, documenting the reflections, emotions, and political sentiments expressed by Tibetans in his memory. Lobga Rangzen self-immolated on July 2, 2026, outside the UN headquarters in New York. In his message, the late martyr strongly condemned China’s repressive policies in occupied Tibet and its ongoing campaign to assimilate and ultimately erase the Tibetan people. He called on fellow Tibetans that restoration of Tibet’s independence is the only lasting solution to end the sufferings endured under China’s colonial occupation. Speaking about the motivation behind compiling the book, Loyak Tashi, who compiled the collection, said the idea emerged within a week of Lobga Rangzen’s passing. During that period, he noticed a growing number of essays and prose pieces being written and circulated online in remembrance of the activist. He said Tsering Logye, the editor of the book, approached him and suggested bringing the writings together in a single volume. The conversation prompted him to undertake the compilation, as he feared that many of the tributes and reflections would gradually disappear from public memory within a year or two. He said the book was therefore intended not only to preserve those writings but also to honour what he described as Lobga Rangzen’s “ultimate sacrifice.” Among the speakers at the launch was Dr Sonam Tobgyal, a researcher at Tibet Watch and an advocate for Tibetan independence, who said he had read most of the pieces in the collection after encountering them on social media. Reflecting on the writings, he said he sensed a renewed expression of support for the Tibetan independence cause among those who had written them. He contrasted this with the situation roughly 15 years ago, when, in his assessment, relatively few Tibetans were paying sustained attention to the independence movement. While acknowledging that activism around Tibetan independence had continued, he said the past decade had been particularly difficult for advocates of the cause. According to his observation, many activists within the Tibetan community have faced challenges while organising campaigns and advocating for independence at both individual and organisational levels. He further noted what he described as a growing distance among some Tibetans from the broader Tibetan cause, particularly at times when international governments offered limited support or when the situation inside Tibet deteriorated. However, he said Lobga Rangzen’s self-immolation appeared to have rekindled a sense of urgency and responsibility among sections of the Tibetan community. He said the act had reminded people of the importance of keeping the Tibetan issue alive and continuing efforts on behalf of Tibet. He also pointed to what he described as a renewed engagement among younger Tibetans, saying that a strong sense of commitment to the independence cause had been largely absent among younger generations for some time. According to him, young Tibetans have often grown up hearing that achieving independence from China is extremely difficult, that China is too powerful, and that Tibetans could benefit by remaining within China. He said discussions about collectively working toward Tibetan independence had consequently received less emphasis in their upbringing and education. He argued that Lobga Rangzen’s self-immolation had helped revive those sentiments across different sections of Tibetan society, with its impact being felt among both younger and older generations. Another speaker at the launch was Rangzen Dhondup, a close friend of the late activist and president of the Dharamshala regional chapter of the Tibetan Youth Congress (TYC). He said he had known Lobga Rangzen for nearly a decade through their shared involvement in the Tibetan cause. Recalling the day of Lobga Rangzen’s self-immolation, Rangzen Dhondup said the late martyr had called him at around 10 a.m. IST. At the time, he was attending the annual general meeting of the TYC in Poanta Sahib and was unable to take the call. He instead sent him a message explaining that he was in a meeting and would call him later. He said he could never have imagined that the missed call would come only hours before Lobga Rangzen set himself on fire. He learnt of the self-immolation from a friend early the following morning and said he initially struggled to believe what had happened. He recalled that Lobga Rangzen had served two consecutive terms with the Tibetan Youth Congress’ New York and New Jersey chapter beginning in 2017, before later becoming involved with the Tibetan National Congress (TNC). Rangzen Dhondup said the two remained in regular contact, frequently discussing campaigns, sharing updates on activities and exchanging ideas on advancing the Tibetan cause. According to him, Lobga Rangzen also consistently supported campaigns organised by the TYC Dharamshala regional chapter, including through financial contributions. He described him as a person deeply committed to preserving Tibetan identity and consistently advocating campaigns in support of Tibetan independence. title: CTA reaffirms democratic legacy on 66th Tibetan Democracy Day
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 2:The exile Tibetan government, officially known as the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA), on Wednesday commemorated the 66th anniversary of Tibetan Democracy Day at the Tsuglagkhang Temple in Dharamshala, reaffirming the democratic institutions established under the visionary leadership of His Holiness the Dalai Lama. The commemoration brought together representatives of the three pillars of the Tibetan democratic system—the CTA President Penpa Tsering and members of his Cabinet, elected members of the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile, and judges of the Tibetan Supreme Justice Commission—along with members of the Tibetan community and 30 Chinese pro-democracy activists. Among the Chinese activists was Dang Yang, a veteran of the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests who was subsequently imprisoned twice by the Chinese Communist government. Addressing the gathering, the Tibetan political leader condemned China’s newly implemented Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, which came into effect on July 1, warning that the legislation and accompanying policies warrant a firm and appropriate response. “These include severe restrictions on the Tibetan language; the falsification of history and identity; forced cultural assimilation at the grassroots level; the Sinicisation of Tibetan Buddhism; enforced ethnic integration; pervasive technological surveillance; political and social coercion; the political vetting of Tibetan cadres; the violation of regional autonomy rights; and the assertion of extraterritorial jurisdiction targeting organisations and individuals worldwide,” the Tibetan leader said. He said the Chinese Communist government’s policies since its colonial occupation of Tibet have consistently sought to undermine Tibetan identity, particularly through restrictions on language, religion, and culture. Urging Tibetans both inside Tibet and in exile to make the preservation of their heritage part of everyday life, he called for greater participation in institutional initiatives to safeguard the Tibetan language and cultural identity. “On our part, it is not enough merely to declare opposition and protest; we must expose and confront these malicious policies based on a well-informed understanding. We therefore urge all Tibetans to join the Central Tibetan Administration in these vital efforts,” he stated. Dang Yang, speaking at the commemoration, described the Tibetan democratic system as a model of democratic resilience and said its experience offered important lessons to China’s pro-democracy movement. “The Tibetan experience has demonstrated to the world that even without a territory under its actual control, without an army, a democratic system can still function successfully and generate powerful political influence,” Dang said. He contrasted the Tibetan exile administration’s democratic legitimacy with what he described as the Chinese Communist Party’s reliance on “violence, lies, and control.” “The Tibetan community in exile, by contrast, relies on the recognition of its people, democratic legitimacy, and the cohesion of its institutions,” he said. Dang sated that the Tibetan democratic system has helped unite Tibetans dispersed across the world and ensured the continuity of their political voice across generations. “It is precisely this democratic system that has brought together Tibetans scattered across the world, generation after generation. It has ensured that the Tibetan voice has not been silenced by the Chinese Communist Party, and that the Party has never been able to represent the Tibetans or determine their future,” he said. Dang also announced plans for the establishment of a China Congress, a proposed democratic representative institution outside the framework of the Chinese Communist Party. He said the initiative has not yet been formally established but has already attracted more than 1,000 founding electors. “We hope to begin a democratic practice belonging to the Chinese people outside the system of the Chinese Communist Party, and to accumulate experience about China’s future democratic transition and constitutional development,” he said. He said China’s democracy movement could draw particularly from the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile’s experience of electoral representation. “The Tibetan experience of election has enabled representatives with a mandate from the electorate to continue making their voices heard in the international community,” Dang said, adding that China’s democracy movement has yet to develop a representative institution with a comparable electoral foundation. Looking ahead to a possible democratic transition in China, Dang said a future Chinese political system must abandon coercive policies towards Tibetans and instead respect their cultural, religious and national identity. “A future democratic China must never again treat Tibetans through oppression or forced assimilation. Instead, it must respect the Tibetan people’s culture, religion, language, national identity, and fundamental rights,” he said. He called for future relations between the Chinese and Tibetan peoples to be founded on equality and peaceful dialogue rather than political domination. Dang further proposed establishing a sustained platform for dialogue between Tibetans and Han Chinese living overseas, covering political and cultural questions related to Tibet as well as the future spiritual and cultural relationship between the two peoples. He concluded by expressing hope that Tibetans and Chinese alike would eventually be free from authoritarian rule and able to determine their own futures. The Tibetan democratic system began taking shape soon after the Dalai Lama arrived in India in exile. The process formally began with the establishment of the Commission of Tibetan People’s Deputies in 1960, followed by the drafting of constitutional frameworks in 1961 and their promulgation in 1963. A major milestone came in 1991 with the adoption of the Charter of Tibetans-in-Exile, which established a democratic system founded on the separation of powers and independent institutions. In 2001, Tibetans began directly electing the head of the Kashag, or Cabinet. A decade later, in 2011, the Dalai Lama devolved his remaining political and administrative authority and transferred it fully to democratically elected Tibetan leaders. title: Tibetan researchers, activists demand transparency from China over Kyirong flash floods
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 1:A joint press briefing in Dharamshala on Tuesday raised alarm over what activists and researchers described as an ‘information blackout’ surrounding the devastating flash floods in Kyirong in occupied Tibet, demanding that China release full and verifiable information on casualties, missing persons, displacement, destruction, and its emergency response. The briefing, titled “Asia’s Water Tower in Crisis: Tibet-Nepal Flash Floods Demand Transparency,” was organised by the International Tibet Network (ITN) and Students for a Free Tibet–India (SFT-India) at the Tibetan Settlement Office (TSO) hall in Dharamshala. The briefing brought together researchers, activists, and a Tibetan monk from Kyirong, including Dhondup Wangmo, Research Fellow at the Environment and Development Desk of the Tibet Policy Institute (TPI), the Central Tibetan Administration’s think tank; Dr Lobsang Yangtso, Senior Environmental Researcher at ITN; Jampa Palden, a monk from Kyirong; and Tashi Dhondup, Campaigns Coordinator at SFT-India. The speakers called on Beijing to provide complete, accurate, and timely information about the scale of the disaster, warning that withholding, manipulating, or selectively releasing information could endanger communities both within occupied Tibet and downstream in Nepal and India. Jampa Palden, who is from Kyirong, shared accounts received from family members in the region, claiming that the entire Lhende area had been severely inundated and that three villages along the Lhende River had been completely washed away. According to his account, each of the three villages was home to at least 30–40 households. He added semi-nomadic Tibetan communities predominantly inhabit the area and is also an important trade corridor linking Tibet with Nepal. Chinese state-controlled media have so far reported 16 deaths and 546 people missing. The discrepancy between limited official reporting and accounts emerging from outside Tibet was cited at the briefing as evidence of the urgent need for independent access and transparent reporting from the disaster zone. Dr Lobsang Yangtso said that while the precise causes and trajectory of the recent glacial outburst have not yet been scientifically established, the disaster should prompt scrutiny of the rapid expansion of infrastructure across the environmentally fragile Himalayan region. She argued that extensive construction of roads, bridges, and hydropower projects in high-risk areas could compound the effects of climate-driven hazards, including glacial lake outburst floods, ice and snow avalanches, and other forms of cryospheric instability. She also pointed to the accelerating effects of climate change on the Tibetan Plateau, describing Tibet as an exceptionally climate-sensitive region. According to figures cited at the briefing, the Tibetan Plateau and Himalayan region contain around 63,000 glaciers, 25,000 glacial lakes, 766 identified glacial-lake flood hazards, and 716 ice- and snow-avalanche hazards. “These risks,” she warned, could pose serious threats to communities in the future, particularly as warming alters the stability of glaciers and high-altitude landscapes. She also drew attention to China’s ongoing construction of a proposed 60-gigawatt hydropower project in Medog County, Nyingtri Prefecture, Tibet, close to India’s Arunachal Pradesh border. She warned that large-scale infrastructure development in such an ecologically sensitive and climate-vulnerable landscape could have ramifications far beyond Tibet and across downstream areas, including India, Nepal, and Bangladesh. The speaker therefore called for an international moratorium on mega-development projects in Tibet, arguing that large projects should not proceed until Tibetans can freely provide or withhold their consent without fear of detention, intimidation, or other forms of repression. She further urged Himalayan countries to consider an immediate moratorium on large hydropower projects until comprehensive climate, environmental and disaster-risk assessments are completed. The briefing also scrutinised the role of multilateral development banks and international financial institutions in financing hydropower projects across the Himalayas. Lobsang Yagntso specifically raised concerns over international financing for the Trishuli River hydropower project in Nepal, arguing that financial institutions must be held accountable when projects proceed despite known glacier-related risks and insufficient environmental assessment. She pointed to the vulnerability of hydropower infrastructure to sudden glacier-related disasters and questioned whether lenders have adequately incorporated increasingly volatile climate and geological conditions into their risk assessments. She argued that financial institutions should not treat Himalayan hydropower projects solely as development or investment opportunities while overlooking their potential consequences for workers, local communities, and downstream populations. The briefing called for independent monitoring, real-time data sharing, and effective cross-border early-warning systems, including timely notification of dangerous glacier movements, glacial lake outbursts, sudden rises in river levels, and other foreseeable hazards. The speakers called on China to grant unhindered access to affected Tibetan areas to international humanitarian organisations, independent journalists, disaster-response agencies, and human rights monitors. They also urged Beijing to ensure that Tibetans who document the disaster or communicate information about the humanitarian situation are not subjected to surveillance, detention, intimidation, prosecution, or other reprisals. The briefing also appealed to international governments, media organisations, humanitarian agencies, and monitoring bodies to use Tibetan place names consistently in official statements, reporting, and documentation. The organisers argued that accurate Tibetan terminology is not merely a linguistic preference but a matter of factual accuracy, cultural respect, and recognition of Tibetan identity. They urged international actors to avoid uncritically adopting Chinese state terminology, including “Xizang,” particularly when reporting on humanitarian, environmental, and human rights issues. title: China censors Kyirong flood footage, grossly under-reports death toll
author: Phayul Newsdesk
content: DHARAMSHALA, Aug. 31: Video footage capturing the terrifying moments when people fled a rapidly advancing wall of mud and debris at the Kyirong Port in occupied Tibet has reportedly been removed from Chinese social-media platforms, fuelling concerns over Beijing’s censorship of information surrounding the devastating Himalayan floods. The footage, which circulated online following the disaster, reportedly shows people scrambling to escape moments before torrents of mud and floodwater engulfed parts of the Kyirong Port. Copies of some of the videos have continued to circulate outside China after the original posts were reportedly deleted. Kyirong County, a strategically important trading gateway between occupied Tibet and Nepal, was among the worst-affected areas on the Tibetan side. The Kyirong Port, a major land crossing, suffered severe damage; roads, buildings, and infrastructure were inundated or swept away. As of Monday, Chinese authorities have reported 16 deaths and 546 people missing in Kyirong County, according to reports citing official figures. By comparison, the death toll on the Nepalese side had risen to 903, with 4,247 people still missing. The stark disparity is particularly striking given that Kyirong was among the areas hardest hit by the catastrophic floods. The figures have intensified scrutiny of the disaster and raised questions about the true scale of casualties in occupied Tibet, where access for independent journalists and observers remains severely restricted. Reports by Indian and international media outlets have stated in their reports that several videos documenting the disaster disappeared from Chinese social-media platforms. Some reports also allege that accounts posting information about casualties and the devastation were removed or restricted. Chinese authorities, however, have rejected allegations that they are suppressing information about the disaster. Authorities have also taken administrative action against people accused of spreading what they described as rumours concerning casualty figures and the scale of the disaster. The reported removal of eyewitness footage is significant because access to Tibet for foreign journalists and independent observers remains highly restricted. In such circumstances, videos recorded by residents, workers, and travellers can provide rare visual evidence of events unfolding in the region. The disappearance of footage has therefore added another layer of controversy to an already catastrophic disaster, particularly as official casualty figures continue to evolve while hundreds remain unaccounted for. Meanwhile, Chinese state media coverage of the disaster has largely centred on rescue and relief operations, repeatedly showcasing images of emergency personnel searching through debris, evacuating residents, and delivering supplies. While such footage documents the ongoing response, the emphasis on rescue efforts, rather than the full extent of the destruction and human toll, has been criticised as presenting a sanitised picture of the catastrophe and potentially obscuring the severity of the disaster on the Tibetan side. The contrast between official coverage and eyewitness footage circulating outside China has further fuelled concerns about information control and the suppression of independent accounts. With hundreds of people still unaccounted for in Kyirong, observers say, the disappearance of videos and restrictions on information could make it increasingly difficult to establish the disaster’s full human cost.
