It states that the legislation promotes population displacement, marginalises the Tibetan language, and separates Tibetans from their ancestral homeland, history, and spiritual traditions. The statement argues that the ultimate objective is to replace distinct Tibetan identity with allegiance to the state-defined "Chinese Nation" (Zhonghua Minzu). It contends that expressions of Tibetan identity, religion, language, and culture could increasingly be treated as political offences or manifestations of "separatism". The signatory Members of the Riigikogu strongly condemn the law, declaring that it possesses "no moral legitimacy in the eyes of the Tibetan people". The statement notes that both the European Parliament and the United Nations have already expressed serious concerns, while arguing that stronger and more decisive international action is urgently needed. The Members of the Riigikogu call on the Government of the PRC to reject the implementation of the law and repeal it. They urge United Nations bodies and mechanisms to review China's assimilation policies and use all available international instruments to prevent further violations of Tibetans' cultural, linguistic, and religious rights. The statement calls for united international diplomatic pressure on Beijing to resolve the China–Tibet conflict peacefully through genuine and mutually respectful dialogue. It expresses support for the Tibetan government in exile in its efforts to preserve and promote Tibetan culture and identity in exile. Tibet Freedom Estonia

title: Tibetans place the confins of over 170 Tibetan self-immolators before UNO and demand freedom for Tibet - Tibet Post International
content: Dharamshala — Tibetans carried the the coffins of over 170 Tibetan self-immolators from Jackson Heights to UN headquarters in New York and along with them marched by hundreds of Tibetans and they protested against the China's illegal occupation of Tibet, implmenting oppressive policies in Tibet, particular China's genocide law (Ethic Unity Law) and demand freedom for Tibet. The Coffin March started from Jackson Heights to UN headquarters in New York, on August 2,2026, to commemorate the one month of passing of the Tibetan martyr Lobga Rangzen, who sacrificed his life by self-immolating, in front of the UN headquarters in New York, on July 2,2026, to call on UN to support justice cause of Tibet, to protest against the Chinese government’s oppressive policies in Tibet including China’s genocide law (Ethic Unity Law) and demand for an independence for Tibet. Tibetans in New York carry the coffins of over 170 Tibetan self-immolators, who sacrificed their lives for a free Tibet and return of His Holiness the Dalai Lama to Tibet. The event was organised by the 19th Regional Tibetan Youth Congress New York/New Jersey, which aims to express their solidarity with all the Tibetan martyrs who sacrificed their lives for Tibet. They said, “we march to honor their courage, remember their sacrifices, and reaffirm our unwavering commitment to the cause of a free Tibet. Their voices will never be forgotten, and their legacy will continue to inspire generations to stand up for truth, justice, and freedom. Free Tibet, Justice for our Martyrs.” Following they reached at the UN headquarters, they placed the confins of over 170 self-immolators in front of UN headquarters and call for justice for them and demand freedom for Tibet. Hundreds of Tibetans from the United States and Canada gathered in front of the United Nations headquarters to commemorate the Tibetan martyrs who sacrificed their lives for a free Tibet and reaffirmed their determination to fight for Tibetan freedom and independence until Tibet is free and His Holiness the Dala Lama returns to Tibet. Several speakers, including the current, former, and regional Presidents of the Tibetan Youth Congress, addressed the crowd, reiterating their commitment to continuing the struggle for a free and independence Tibet, called for unity among Tibetans. Tibetan Youth Congress issued the following demands to the Chinese government, the United Nations, and the international community: 1. United Nations Response: As Lobga Rangzen made the ultimate sacrifice in front of the United Nations Headquarters, we urge the United Nations to respond in a meaningful and formal manner by addressing the grave human rights situation in Tibet and the circumstances that compelled his sacrifice. 2. Accountability for Tibetans Driven to Self-Immolation: The Chinese government must be held accountable for the policies and repression that have driven Lobga Rangzen and numerous Tibetans to the tragic act of self-immolation. 3. Recognition of Tibet's Sovereignty: Tibet was an independent nation before its occupation by the so called People's Republic of China and remains under Chinese occupation today. We call upon the international community to recognize Tibet's historical status and support the Tibetan people's right to restore their freedom and independence. 4. Repeal the so-called “Ethnic Unity and Progress Law”: We reject this law as an instrument of forced assimilation and call for its immediate repeal and the cessation of its implementation throughout Tibet. 5. Immediate and Unconditional Release of All Political Prisoners: We demand the immediate and unconditional release of the world's youngest Tibetan political prisoner 11th Panchen lama, along with all imprisoned environmental activists, Tibetan artists, human rights defenders, and all other political prisoners without conditions and delay. Tibetan Youth Congress said, "A government cannot legislate away the identity of a nation. A policy aimed at erasing people's language, culture, history, and spiritual heritage is not unity, it is a state enforced assimilation. "We reject and condemn the recent statement made by Mr. Stéphane Dujarric, spokesperson of the UN Secretary-General referring to Tibet as a "minority." Such characterization is historically inaccurate narrative, politically incorrect and serves only to reinforce the Chinese Communist Party's propaganda. Tibet is not a minority of China. It is an occupied nation. Calling Tibet a "minority" erases its national identity and undermines the Tibetan people's right to freedom and independence. "We call on the United Nations to uphold truth and impartiality. It must not use language that legitimizes China's occupation of Tibet or erases the Tibetan national identity. The United Nations' words shape global opinion. They must not legitimize occupation or contribute to the erasure of Tibet's identity and the Tibetan people's aspirations for Independence. "The sacrifice of Martyr Lobga Rangzen is not the end of our struggle, it is a renewed call for resistance, solidarity, and international action. His courage has become a symbol of the unbreakable spirit of the Tibetan. Until Tibet is free, his voice will continue to live through our movement, our actions, and our unwavering commitment to justice." Tibet UNHRC Free Tibet

title: A Tribute to Australian Senator Derryn Hinch: A Courageous Voice for Tibet and Justice - Tibet Post International
content: Dharamshala — Australian Senator Derryn Hinch will be remembered not only as one of Australia's most fearless investigative journalists and broadcasters, but also as a parliamentarian who demonstrated the courage to speak publicly on behalf of oppressed peoples. Throughout his distinguished career, he became widely known as the "Human Headline" for his unwavering commitment to exposing injustice, defending victims, and holding those in positions of power to account. Australian Senator and media personality Derryn Hinch passed away peacefully in his sleep at his home in Melbourne on 10 July 2026, at the age of 82. His death marked the end of an extraordinary public life spanning more than six decades in journalism, broadcasting, and politics. Known as the “Human Headline”, Hinch was remembered for his distinctive voice, fearless advocacy, and determination to speak on issues he believed required public attention. Among the many causes that Senator Hinch supported during his time in public life was the cause of Tibet. As leader of an Australian parliamentary delegation that visited Dharamshala, India, from 20 to 23 November 2017, he witnessed first-hand the resilience, dignity, and determination of the Tibetan people living in exile. The delegation also included the Hon. Kevin Andrews MP, Senator Kimberley Kitching, and Meryl Swanson MP, reflecting bipartisan Australian parliamentary engagement with the Tibetan issue. During the visit, Senator Hinch met His Holiness the Dalai Lama and senior representatives of the Central Tibetan Administration. He also visited Tibetan educational and cultural institutions, gaining a deeper understanding of the challenges faced by Tibetans both inside Tibet and in exile. Speaking at a press conference in Dharamshala, Senator Hinch expressed admiration for the Tibetan people's steadfast commitment to preserving their identity despite decades of hardship. Referring to China's demographic policies in Tibet, he remarked that attempts to overwhelm the Tibetan population had failed because the Tibetan people had refused to surrender their identity, culture, and hope. He praised their resilience and expressed confidence that their determination and commitment to peaceful dialogue would continue to sustain their struggle. Senator Derryn Hinch expressed his admiration for the resilience and determination of the people of Tibet. Reflecting on China's policies in Tibet, he remarked, "The Chinese... have this different version of 'populate or perish'... through the Han and the other people who would populate Tibet in the hope that you will perish—and you aren't perishing." He praised the Tibetan people's strength and commitment to peaceful dialogue, adding, "We've seen signs here, your background, your backbone and your passion will see you through the Middle Way." Senator Hinch also observed that many democratic nations were becoming more willing to engage openly with the Tibet issue, stating, "You'll find, going back a few years Western nations were sometimes worried that if we meet with the Dalai Lama, will that affect our economic ties with China. I think those days are over." Senator Hinch also observed that international attitudes towards Tibet were evolving. He noted that many democratic nations had previously been reluctant to engage openly with His Holiness the Dalai Lama for fear of jeopardising economic relations with China. In his view, however, those concerns were beginning to diminish as governments increasingly recognised the importance of defending universal values, including human rights, freedom, and justice. The parliamentary delegation collectively called for continued international attention to the situation in Tibet. Members urged that the issue should not be forgotten and stressed the importance of maintaining peaceful international pressure to achieve a just and lasting resolution through dialogue. Their visit demonstrated that support for Tibet transcended political party affiliations and reflected shared democratic values within Australia's Parliament. For Tibetans around the world, Senator Hinch's willingness to visit the Tibetan exile community, listen to their experiences, and speak publicly about their aspirations represented an important act of solidarity. His engagement helped bring greater visibility to a cause that has often struggled to receive sustained international attention. Although Senator Derryn Hinch is widely remembered for his fearless journalism, advocacy for victims' rights, and distinguished parliamentary service, his support for Tibet also deserves recognition. He showed that principled leadership requires the courage to speak for those whose voices are too often ignored. His legacy reminds us that freedom, justice, human dignity, and compassion remain universal values worthy of defence. The Tibetan people, together with many supporters of human rights around the world, will remember Senator Derryn Hinch with gratitude and respect for standing beside them during an important chapter in their modern history.

title: A massive earthquake strikes Tibet, hundreds die, His Holiness offers prayer - Tibet Post International
content: Dharamshala — A devastating 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck Dingri and neighboring Shigatse counties in Tibet on Tuesday morning, killing 126 Tibetans, and injuring 188 and destroying 3609 homes. His Holiness the Dalai Lama, the leaders of the CTA, Tibetans inside the Tibet and in exile, the French President and the Taiwanese President express their solidarity and extend their prayers to the victims of the disaster. On January 7, 2025, at around 9:05 a.m. local time, a devastating magnitude 7.1 earthquake struck Dingri County (Ch: Tingri), as residents woke up to temperatures of -13°C. This sudden catastrophe has left the population distraught and in disarray. Thousands of homes have been destroyed, along with water and electricity networks. This earthquake also affects Dingri County and Shigatse's neighboring counties, such as Tingkye County, Lhatse County, Sakya County and Ngamring County. According to US Geological Survey data, the 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck Dingri and neighboring Shigatse counties in Tibet. But the Chinese government claimed it was only a magnitude 6.8 earthquake. The Chinese government is still trying to hide the truth, and the number of Tibetans killed and injured could also be inaccurate. After hearing sad news from Tibet, His Holiness the Dalai Lama expresses deep sadness over the Earthquake in Tibet, His Holiness wrote on January 7, 2025, “I am deeply saddened to learn of the devastating earthquake that struck Dingri in Tibet and the surrounding regions this morning. It has caused the tragic loss of many lives, numerous injuries, and extensive destruction to homes and property.” “I offer my prayers for those who have lost their lives and extend my wishes for a swift recovery to all who have been injured,” he concluded. Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile (TPiE)also issued condolence statement regarding the devasting earthquake in Tibet, on January 7, 2025. The statement wrote, “an earthquake measuring 7.1 on the Richter scale struck several regions of Tibet, including the Dingri region, on the morning of 7 January 2025. Reports indicate that over a hundred people have lost their lives or been injured, with extensive damage to homes. The harsh winter conditions exacerbate the suffering, leaving many without adequate food, clothing, and shelter. This tragedy is deeply saddening and of great concern.” “His Holiness the Dalai Lama, along with spiritual leaders from all Buddhist traditions, is offering prayers for the souls of those who have passed. The Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile joins in these prayers, seeking the blessings of Avalokiteshvara for the deceased. We extend our heartfelt condolences to the grieving families and pray for the swift recovery of the injured, hoping they will receive timely and appropriate medical care,” they said. “We also call upon both public and private sectors to provide urgent assistance to those facing housing and other critical needs in the aftermath of this devastating disaster,” TPiE said. Addressing the earthquake, Sikyong Penpa Tsering remarked, “Tibet is prone to earthquakes due to its location on the collision boundary between the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates. This region, part of the Himalayan seismic belt, experiences significant geological activity as the Indian plate pushes northward under the Eurasian plate, resulting in seismic events.” Highlighting the importance of ecological preservation, Sikyong emphasised, “The Chinese government must pay greater attention to Tibet’s fragile environment. This is not only about protecting Tibet’s ecology but also about safeguarding the well-being of its neighbouring countries like India and the rest of Asia. Furthermore, China’s plan to construct the world’s largest dam poses a significant threat to Tibet’s environment and its neighbouring regions.” Sikyong concluded by urging the Chinese government to prioritise the future and take proactive measures to preserve Tibet’s unique environment, which has far-reaching implications for the region and the world.” The CTA, alongside Tibetans in and around Dharamshala, will organise a prayer service on January 8, 2025, at the Tsuglagkhang Main Temple. Chief Minister Shri Pema Khandu ji posted on X: "I am deeply saddened by the devastating earthquake along the Tibet-Nepal border. The loss of lives and destruction is heartbreaking. My sincere condolences to the families who lost their loved ones. May the departed souls rest in peace. We pray for the safety of all affected and wish the injured a swift recovery." Taiwan President Lai Ching-te posted on X: "We stand with the people of Tibet and neighboring regions affected by the devastating earthquake. Our deepest condolences to the families who lost loved ones, and we hope rescue and aid efforts quickly reach all those in need." French President Emmanuel Macron posted on X: "France extends its condolences to those who lost loved ones in the devastating earthquake in Tibet, and stands ready to support affected communities across the Himalayan region." The Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs posted on official X account: "We extend our deepest sympathies to those affected by the devastating earthquake in Tibet. Our condolences to all who lost loved ones, and we commend the courage of rescue workers during this crisis." Tibet Tibetans earthquake

title: The New Chinese law mandates assimilation of Tibetans into Han Culture - Tibet Post International
content: Dharamshala — The new Chinese law recently adopted by the People's Republic of China, which targets the Tibetan language, identity, culture, and religion as part of a policy of Sinicization, mandates the assimilation of Tibetans into Chinese culture through parents, monasteries, and public institutions; it will take effect on July 1, 2026. The National People's Congress (NPC) passed a law on March 12, 2026, titled “Promotion of Ethnic Unity and Progress in the People's Republic of China (PRC).” This law reinforces policies of “Sinicization” and “assimilation,” particularly with regard to Tibetans and other oppressed peoples of Mongolia and East Turkestan. It mandates the Sinicization and assimilation of the Tibetan people, using parents, monasteries, various social organizations, and state institutions as instruments of implementation; the law is scheduled to officially take effect on July 1, 2026. The new law aims to codify Xi Jinping’s policy on ethnic affairs, which promotes greater integration and cultural assimilation under the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) regime. It prioritizes the use of Mandarin in education, public services, and public life, thereby replacing previous policies that allowed instruction in minority languages such as Tibetan, Uyghur, and Mongolian. It also requires religious practices to align with Han-centered Chinese cultural norms and socialist values through the “Sinicization” of religion. The law also requires parents and teachers to indoctrinate children so that they “love the CCP and China as a nation” and “internalize the idea that the Chinese people form one big family,” while warning against any attempt to instill in children concepts related to their own Tibetan culture, religion, and customs. It forces Tibetan parents to perform additional tasks during their children’s summer and winter vacations. The Chinese new law further encouraged the inter-ethnic marriage, which aims to marry Tibetans and other ethnic people to Han Chinese and make their wives, husbands and children into Chinese. Article 2 of the new law imposes the ideas of Chinese leaders such as Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, and Xi Jinping on the population, particularly on Tibetan children and Tibetans. The law also requires the population to raise Chinese flags and display Chinese cultural symbols everywhere, even among truck drivers working in the field. It recently banned Tibetan cultural symbols such as thangkas and hats, which shows that the Chinese government is deeply insecure and is trying to physically demonstrate that these people are citizens of the nation, yet it fails to impose Chinese culture on Tibetans, no matter what methods are used. Article 5 of the new law states: “All citizens of the People’s Republic of China are equal before the law. All ethnic groups in the People’s Republic of China are equal. Any discrimination or oppression against an ethnic group is prohibited,” however, Tibetans and other oppressed peoples are constantly subjected to discrimination in their professional lives, at their workplaces, when traveling, at school, and even when trying to book a hotel room, as hotels refuse to accommodate Tibetans. Article 15 of the law requires Tibetans to “fully promote the use of the nation’s common language (Mandarin) and script” and stipulates that “the use of the nation’s common language and its script shall not be obstructed by any organization or individual.” It forces Tibetans and other oppressed peoples to learn and use the Chinese language and script, and to abandon their own language and script. This article stipulates that schools and other educational institutions must use the Chinese language and script as the primary language of instruction; this forces teachers and students to learn Chinese without any alternative and compels them to do so; it aims to make Tibetans and other non-Chinese populations lose their language, culture, and religion, and to assimilate them into Chinese culture. Article 20 of the law compels Tibetan parents to instill in their children thougts such as “love for the Chinese Communist Party, the motherland, the people, and the Chinese people,” and to encourage them to embrace the idea that the Chinese people form one single family; it also prohibits teaching Tibetan children their own language, culture, and religion, which constitutes a violation of their law and the fundamental rights of Tibetans. Article 46 of the law requires Tibetan monasteries to carry out activities aimed at the Sinicization of Buddhism, to instill in Tibetan monks the communist ideas of Chinese leaders in the name of “patriotism,” and to promote “ethnic, religious, and social harmony.” Article 60 of the law warns social groups, businesses, institutions, and other social organizations against any actions that could undermine the new law; if they do not cease such activities, they face penalties. It also warns these groups against any activity aimed at “dividing the nation”—an accusation often leveled against Tibetans who have organized peaceful protests against the Chinese government’s oppressive policies toward the Tibetan people, language, and religion. Following the passage of this law, criticism was voiced by the international community, academics, and human rights organizations, who stated that the law constituted an instrument of “forced assimilation” that could infringe upon the cultural, linguistic, and religious rights of Tibetans, Uyghurs, and Inner Mongolians. Some see this as a reversal of previous policies that granted only nominal regional autonomy. Even before the new Chinese law officially took effect, Chinese authorities in Tibetan regions had already begun removing Tibetan-language signs from school gates, shops, and offices as early as March 15, 2026. These actions are evidence of the illegal and ruthless measures taken by the Chinese authorities against the Tibetan people, their language, culture, and religion, and are aimed at erasing Tibetan identity. Tibet Language Identity

title: Tibetans mourn death of Lobga Rangzen, protest China’s repressive policies in Tibet - Tibet Post International
content: Dharamshala — Tibetans in Canada, the United States, Europe, India and Taiwan have organised demonstrations to pay tribute to the great sacrifice of Lobga Rangzen, a Tibetan independence activist, who self-immolated in front of the UN headquarters to protest against the People’s Republic of China’s oppressive policies in Tibet and to demand an independence for Tibet, as he said, "cause of all problems for Tibetans are lack of an independence for Tibet." Human Rights network for Tibet and Taiwan, Tibet Religious Foundation of His Holiness the Dalai Lama, Taiwan Association for Human Rights and several Taiwanese civil society organisations jointly organised a memorial service at 7PM, local time, on July 15, 2026, to pay tribute of Lobga Rangzen , who self-immolated in protest against the Chinese Communist Party’s so-called ‘Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress’. Tibetans, activists from Tibet, Tibet-support NGOs, Hong Kong, East Turkestan and Taiwan—all affected by the CCP’s so-called “ethical unity law”, gathered at Liberty Square in Taipei, Taiwan, at local time, 7 PM, on July 15,2026, to mourn Lobga Rangzen, who self-immolated in front of UN headquarters in New York on July 2,2026, to protest against the Chinese government’s crackdown and oppressive policies in Tibet. The activists also protested against the CCP’s law aimed at eliminating identities of Tibetans and other oppressed people. As Lobga Rangzen had said, the struggle must go on; thus, this gathering was not merely a tribute but, above all, an affirmation of "unity"—uniting to resist the tyranny of the CCP and uniting to oppose this harmful law. The activists wrote, "The Tibetan martyr Lobga Rangzen (རང་བཙན་བློ་དགའ) real name Lobsang Palden; Rangzen means ‘independence’ in Tibetan) self-immolated at 5.59 pm (ET) on July 2, 2026, in front of the main entrance to the United Nations Headquarters in New York, holding the Tibetan national flag, in protest against Chinese tyranny and to appeal for the attention of the international community. This footage, streamed live from Loga Rangzen’s Facebook account, it breaks the hearts not only of Tibetans but of anyone with a conscience who witnesses it. The agony of being engulfed by flames is clinically recognised as one of the most intense and unbearable forms of pain—a torment that transcends human physiological limits—yet he remained standing upright until he collapsed at the very last moment." Why did Lobga Rangzen, living in a free country, choose such an extreme form of protest—setting himself on fire to offer his body as a sacrifice for the cause of Tibet? On July 1, 2026, the CCP implemented the so-called "Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress," Lobga Rangzen set himself on fire on July 2, 2026, to protest against the law. These were his final words: “What we are doing today is preserving our language and our culture. That is why we must continue to dance when it is time to dance, and to sing when it is time to sing. For the purpose of all this is to enable the younger generation of Tibetans to embrace and pass on their own language and culture. We must not remain prisoners of grief or silence simply because of the actions of a single person. What we should truly mourn—is the loss of our own country (Tibet). Each of us should commit ourselves more fully to our cause. That is why, with my hands joined in prayer, I implore all of you: if you truly wish to mourn me, act in accordance with the wishes I have expressed here. I don’t want you to mourn for me, I want you to continue the struggle for Tibetan independence, because the lack of independence of Tibet is the root of all our problems. Bhoe Gyalo, Bhoe Rangzen Gyalo” [Victory to Tibet. Victory to Tibetan Independence]." The Tibetan activits said, "Since 2009, there have been 159 self-immolations within Tibet; of these, 127 individuals are known to have died, while the fate of most of the others—who were forcibly taken away by military police—remains unknown. Outside Tibet (in India, Nepal, and the United States), a total of 11 Tibetans have self-immolated. The cumulative global total stands at 170 known cases, though there may be unreported incidents. While early self-immolators were primarily monks and nuns, the practice subsequently spread to all strata of Tibetan society—including nomads, farmers, students, intellectuals, mothers, and popular singers (such as Tsewang Norbu, who died by self-immolation in 2022)—with ages ranging from 15 to 81. The slogans shouted and the final messages or letters left behind by these individuals centered on key demands: the return of His Holiness the Dalai Lama to Tibet, the need for Tibetan freedom, and protests against the Chinese Communist Party’s forced policies of Sinicization—which are driving the cultural extermination of Tibet—along with a desire to preserve Tibetan religion, language, and culture." "These self-immolators were not driven by personal despair; rather, they sacrificed themselves through this extreme form of non-violence—an act that is peaceful and harms no one but the self—in an attempt to ignite international attention regarding the suffering of Tibet and to awaken a sense of unity among the Tibetan people," they added. ​ "We cannot bear to see—nor do we wish for—any more Tibetans sacrificing themselves in this way; the best course of action is for the world to heed the demands of the self-immolators and resist the atrocities committed by the Chinese Communist Party," the Tibetans urged. Hundreds of Tibetans rallied in the streets of Mysuru and Bengaluru, in India, on July 15, 2025, to mark the second week of the death of Lobga Rangzen, a Tibetan independence activist who self-immolated in front of the UN headquarters to protest against the People’s Republic of China’s oppressive policies in Tibet and to demand independence for Tibet. These peaceful demonstrators put forward three demands: the repeal of the so-called "Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress," and the oppressive measures in Tibet; the closure of colonial-style boarding schools that targeting Tibetan children; and to pay tribute to Lobga Rangzen. Tibetans, supporters of Tibet and the Tibetan Association of Germany, in collaboration with the Tibetan Initiative in Germany, organised a solidarity demonstration and protest outside the Chinese Embassy in Berlin, on July 15, 2026, to pay tribute to the Tibetan martyr Lobga Rangzen, who self-immolated to protest against the ongoing oppression of the Tibetan people and against the PRC's so-called "Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress." Tibet Independence

title: Tibetans vehemently protest against the PRC's so-called "ethnic unity law" - Tibet Post International
content: Dharamshala — Hundreds of Tibetans staged a vigorous protest outside the United Nations headquarters in New York—the site where Tibetan independence activist Lobga Rangzen had self-immolated. He protested against the PRC's oppressive policies in Tibet, particularly the so-called "Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress," and to demand independence for Tibet, he asserted that "the lack of independence for Tibet is the root cause of all the problems that Tibetan people are facing." The Regional Tibetan Youth Congress of New York and New Jersey (RTYCNYNJ) organised a protest outside the United Nations headquarters and the Chinese Consulate in New York on July 16, 2026, to pay tribute to Tibetan martyr Lobsang Palden (or Lobga Rangzen) and commemorate the two weeks following his death, who self-immolated to protest against the People's Republic of China's oppressive policies in Tibet, particularly the so-called "Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress," and to demand independence for Tibet. Hundreds of Tibetans took part in the demonstration; they carried Lobga Rangzen’s coffin and protested outside the United Nations headquarters and the Chinese consulate in New York. They chanted slogans such as: "UN, wake up," "UN, speak for Tibet," "World leaders, wake up," "World leaders, speak up for Tibet," "China lies, Tibetans die," "We want justice for Lobga Rangzen," "Lobga Rangzen’s life matters," "Lobga Rangzen died for a free Tibet," "We want justice for Tibetans," "Shame on the UN," "China is guilty, guilty of genocide," and "Stop the cultural genocide in Tibet." Then the peaceful protesters marched from the United Nations headquarters to the Chinese consulate in New York, where they staged a vigorous protest, chanting slogans such as "Tibet is not part of China," "China, get out of Tibet—Tibet is an independent country," "Tibet belongs to Tibetans"and "The Tibetan people do not recognise the legitimacy of Chinese rule or the laws imposed on Tibet," A representative of RTYCNYNJ read out the open letter of Central Tibetan Youth Congress to the gathering. Which states, "This is not merely a letter. It is a message carried by the final sacrifice of Tibetan patriot Lobga Rangzen, whose body was engulfed in flames because our homeland had been occupied and our people deprived of their freedom. His last act was not one of despair, it was one of resistance. he raised the Tibetan National Flag and he stood on fire, and declared to the world: "Free Tibet, China Out of Tibet." "He sacrificed himself for the cause of Tibet and its Independence because decades of political repression, cultural destruction, restrictions on religious freedom, transnational repression, and now the implementation of the so-called "Ethnic Unity Law." "You call it a law of unity. In reality you are trying to legalize the genocide, a legal procedure design to erase the identity of oppressed people. A law that weakens a nation's language, religion, culture, and history cannot be called unity. Unity cannot be imposed through assimilation. Unity cannot be manufactured through fear. Unity without freedom is not unity at all. "The Chinese government must recognize the legitimate aspiration of the Tibetan people and restore Tibet's independence. Lasting peace and stability cannot be achieved through repression, forced assimilation, or military control, but only by ending occupation and respecting the will of the Tibetan people. We urge China to choose justice over oppression, freedom over domination, and peace over continued confrontation." The Tibetan activists also managed to deliver a letter to the Chinese embassy, ​​demanding full independence for Tibet and calling on the Chinese government to end its oppressive policies and ethnic cleansing law in Tibet. Tibet Human Rights Free Tibet

title: "USA and Great Britain considered Tibet to be an independent state": Frances C. Cutler - Tibet Post International
content: Dharamshala — Tibet Museum organised an exhibition titled "Frontier Diplomacy: Britain, Tibet, and Sir Basil Gould", who served as the British representative in Sikkim, Bhutan, and Tibet from 1935 to 1945. Frances C. Cutler, granddaughter of Sir Basil Gould at the exhibition declared, "the documents demonstrating that in 1947, both the United States and Great Britain considered Tibet to be an independent, sovereign state." The Tibet Museum organised an exhibition titled "Frontier Diplomacy: Britain, Tibet, and Sir Basil Gould" at the Tibet Museum in Gankyi (Dharamshala) on April 3, 2026. Sikyong Penpa Tsering of the Central Tibetan Administration and Frances C. Cutler, granddaughter of Sir Basil Gould, inaugurated the exhibition. The exhibition featured two original letters, issued jointly by His Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama and Taktak Pandita Hothokthu and addressed to Gould; these letters request assistance in financial exchange and trade-related matters. Moreover, the exhibition presented rare documentary evidence of diplomatic engagement and Tibetan agency articulated in their own voice. Sir Basil John Gould served as the British Representative to Sikkim, Bhutan, and Tibet from 1935 to 1945. He held the post of British Trade Agent in Gyantse, Tibet, from 1912 to 1913. He personally experienced and participated in the delicate diplomatic maneuvers that preceded the Simla Conference (1913–1914). In 1940, Gould attended the enthronement ceremony of His Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama in Lhasa, Tibet, and bore witness to Tibet's existence as an independent country. Sir Basil John Gould describes his first meeting with His Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama during his enthronement,on February 22, 1940, "As I knelt before the child (14th Dalai Lama), a long white scart which he had blessed was placed round my neck and I felt two small Arm hands on my head. Through those small hands I felt an inner strength, as though some of the strength and wisdom of many Dalai Lamas was being imparted to me." In 1913, at the request of the 13th Dalai Lama and the government of British India, Gould escorted four young Tibetans—Wangdu Norbu Kyipup, Khyenrab Kunzang Mondo, Sonam Gonpa Gongkar, and Rigzin Dorje Ringang—to England so that they might receive an education there. Ringang, who trained as an engineer and subsequently built Tibet's first hydroelectric power plant in 1927. Gongkar trained from British military training, notably at the Royal Military Academy in Woolwich during the First World War. Tenzin Topden, the Director of The Tibet Museum said, "this exhibition examines a pivotal chapter in Tibet's modern history through the life and records of Sir Basil John Gould CBE (1883-1956), a British civil servant whose sustained engagement with Tibet positioned him at the intersection of diplomacy, cultural exchange, and historical documentation. Beyond his official responsibilities, Gould developed a close observational understanding of Tibetan society, leaving behind written and visual records that remain significant sources for the study of twentieth-century Tibet." "A focal point of the exhibition is a group of objects directly associated with Basil Gould, most notably two original letters jointly issued by His Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama and Taktak Pandita Hothokthu. Addressed to Gould, these letters request assistance in financial exchange from the America and other trade-related matters. As the exhibition's principal artefacts, they represent rare documentary evidence of diplomatic engagement and Tibetan agency articulated in their own voice. The concluding section moves beyond archival material to contemporary interpretation," he explained. Topdhen said, "Digital works and an immersive installation-developed in collaboration with Sherab Gatsel Lobling school, differently abled and rehabilitation centre members of the Tibetan community-revisit the enthronement of His Holiness through a large-scale collective collage. These works emphasise history as a living continuum, open to reflection, reinterpretation, and renewed meaning." "The narrative extends into the present through recorded meetings between Basil Gould's grand daughter and His Holiness the Dalai Lama. This ongoing relationship underscores that the preservation of Tibet's history is not solely an act of safeguarding the past, but a commitment to sustaining an accurate, ethical, and uncensored historical memory for future generations," the Director of The Tibet Museum concluded. Frances C. Cutler, granddaughter of Sir Basil Gould said, "Sadly, I never knew my grandfather, as he died two years before I was born, but his life has had a profound and lasting influence on mine. I grew up in rural Hampshire in southern England, far removed from Tibet both physically and culturally. Yet the history and spirit of that distant land surrounded me. As a small child, I ran along an upstairs corridor lined with thangkas, loving the sound of their wooden poles clanking gently against the walls, though some of the fierce deities unsettled me. Above our sitting room fireplace hung Kanwal Krishna's oil portrait of His Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama at his installation in 1940. Around the house were Krishna's watercolours of members of the Holy Family and the ceremony itself. To me, this seemed entirely ordinary." "At the age of eight, I chose to write a school project about the search for the reincarnation of the 14th Dalai Lama. I was fascinated by how the search party was guided to the correct region of Tibet, to the exact house, and how the young boy identified the former Dalai Lama's belongings from among similar objects. I could write about this because I had read my grandfather's book, The Jewel in the Lotus. His account of the four-year-old child sitting so still, day after day, and the quiet awe he inspired, moved me deeply then and still does now. My interest in Tibet deepened when my parents welcomed Tibetan students into our home while they studied in England. I suspect my father was, consciously or not, following in his own father's footsteps, recalling how Sir Basil escorted four "Rugby boys" from Lhasa to England in 1913. Nyima, Chimey, Lobsang, Yangchen and Tsering lived with us, offering kindness, laughter and companionship. Tsering Shakya is now a respected historian at the University of British Columbia, and it has been a joy to reconnect with him," she said. Frances C. Cutler said, "After the death of my parents, Dick and Erica Gould, my curiosity about Sir Basil's life was renewed. Sorting through their papers led me to explore his journeys into Tibet, his work on the Tibetan language, and his ten-year service as Political Officer in Sikkim, Bhutan and Tibet from 1935 to 1945. Margaret Williamson's memoir of her time in Tibet, Sikkim and Bhutan helped me imagine those six-week journeys to Lhasa in the 1930s." "After being approached by the Tibet Office in London, I had the great pleasure of handing them over to Sikyong Penpa Tsering in July last year. It is absolutely wonderful to see them exhibited here (Dharamshala), where they should be, demonstrating that in 1947, both the United States and Great Britain considered Tibet to be an independent, sovereign state," she concluded her speech. Sikyong Penpa Tsering thanked Frances C. Cutler for her donation and elaborated on the historical engagements of the independent Tibetan government with Western nations. The Sikyong highlighted the long tradition of visits by Western nationals to Tibet—dating back to the early 17th century—viewing this as evidence of Tibet's historical status, as well as a means to counter China's distorted narratives regarding Tibet's history prior to its annexation by the People's Liberation Army in 1950s. Tibet Tibetans History Britain

title: His Holiness the Dalai Lama congratulates Andy Burnham, the new PM of the UK - Tibet Post International
content: Dharamshala — His Holiness the Dalai Lama congratulated Andy Burnham on his assumption of the office of Prime Minister of the UK. His Holiness wrote, "I wish you every success in meeting the challenges that lie ahead in fulfilling the needs and aspirations of the British people, and in contributing to the creation of a more peaceful and compassionate world for us all." His Holiness the Dalai Lama wrote to Andy Burnham on July 21, 2026, from the Shewatsel Phodrang in Leh, Ladakh (India), to congratulate him on taking office as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. Andy Burnham assumed office as the 57th Prime Minister of the United Kingdom on July 20, 2026, after meeting with King Charles III at Buckingham Palace to form a new government, succeeding Sir Keir Starmer. His Holiness the Dalai Lama wrote,"Today, the world is passing through a very difficult and uncertain time. Historically, your country has played a leadership role in international affairs, and it is my hope that even as you work for the development of your own nation, you will also work closely with other countries to resolve the problems before us — both urgent and long-term — with a firm belief in the oneness of humanity and a shared desire for peace and happiness." The spiritual leader of Tibet said, “As you may be aware, we Tibetans have long enjoyed a historic and unique relationship with your country. During my several visits there, I have deeply appreciated the warmth extended to me by people from all walks of life, as well as their support for my efforts to promote human values, nonviolence, and interfaith harmony.” “I wish you every success in meeting the challenges that lie ahead in fulfilling the needs and aspirations of the British people, and in contributing to the creation of a more peaceful and compassionate world for us all,"His Holiness concluded his congratulatory letter. Tibet Dalai Lama

title: Thousands of Tibetans staged protest to condenm PRC's "Ethic Unity Law" - Tibet Post International
content: Dharamshala — Thousands of Tibetans staged a strong protest against the Chinese government’s repressive policies in Tibet, particular to China's so-called "Ethnic Unity and Progress Law" and they said, "this law is an illegal instrument to institutionalize the Chinese government's long-standing policy of forced assimilation and to strengthen state control over non-Chinese peoples, particularly Tibetans." They also expressed solidarity with Tibetan martyr Lobga Rangzen, who self-immolated to protest against the PRC's oppressive policies in Tibet and to demand independence for Tibet. The Tibetan Youth Congress, the Tibetan Women's Association, Students for a Free Tibet – India, Gu-Chu-Sum Movement of Tibet, National Democratic Party of Tibet, and the International Tibet Network, organised a joint protest honoring the supreme sacrifice of Martyr Lobga Rangzen and condemning China's so-called "Ethnic Unity and Progress Law." The protest joined by thousands of Tibetans around the Dharamshala and they marched from McLeod Ganj to Kachari, Dharamshala, on July 18, 2026. The Tibetan organisations and protestors call on the United Nations and the international community to recognise martyr Lobga Rangzen's sacrifice, address the worsening human rights situation in Tibet, reject China's policy of forced assimilation, and support the Tibetan people's right to freedom. When Tibetan protestors marching from gate of Tsuklakhang, Mecleod to Police Groud, Kacheri, Dharamshala, they carried Lobga Rangzen’s coffin and protested against the Chinese government's repressive policies in Tibet. They chanted slogans such as: "UNO, wake up," "UNO, speak for Tibet," "World leaders, wake up," "World leaders, speak up for Tibet," "China lies, Tibetans die," "We want justice for Lobga Rangzen," "Lobga Rangzen’s life matters," "Lobga Rangzen died for a free Tibet," "We want justice for Tibetans," "Shame on the UNO," "China is guilty, guilty of genocide," and "Stop the cultural genocide in Tibet." Tsering Dolma, President of Tibetan Women's Association read out the statement of above Tibetan NGOs in English, she said, "Recent on July 2, 2026, Tibetan patriot Lobga Rangzen set himself on fire in front of the United Nations Headquarters in New York in a profound act of sacrifice for Tibet and its people. In his final video testament, he made clear that his action was not driven by personal despair, but by his deep concern for the survival of the Tibetan nation. He warned that the Chinese government is carrying out policies aimed at destroying the Tibetan people through systematic repression and the eradication of Tibetan identity." "Lobga Rangzen emphasized that no nation has ever succeeded without commitment, courage, and action for freedom movement. He appealed to Tibetans everywhere to unite and work on the common cause of Tibet's independence. In his testament, Lobga Rangzen stated that we Tibetans lost our fundamental rights and freedoms because we lost our country Tibet. He called upon the Tibetan Government in Exile, the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile, Tibetan civil society organisations, and Tibetans around the world to unite and work collectively for the future of Tibet," she added. "He also requested that his sacrifice should not lead to the cancellation of cultural performances, songs, or other expressions of Tibetan identity, emphasizing that these are essential to preserving Tibetan culture and inspiring younger generations. He asked Tibetans not to mourn his death but instead to fulfill the aspirations for which he sacrificed his life. His final words were: "Victory to Tibet! Victory for Tibet’s Independence!" Tsering Chophel, President of Tibetan Youth Congress said,"On March 12, 2026, during the National People's Congress, the Chinese Communist government adopted the so-called “Regulations on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress”, a 65-article law that entered into force on July 1,2026, coinciding with the anniversary of the founding of the Chinese Communist Party. Presented under the language of "ethnic unity," this law is an illegal instrument to institutionalize the Chinese government's long-standing policy of forced assimilation and to strengthen state control over non-Chinese peoples, particularly Tibetans. "The implementation of this law represents a serious escalation of China's efforts to erase the distinct identity of the Tibetan people. Through the systematic assimilation of language, religion, culture, customs, history, and education, it seeks to transform Tibet into an inseparable part of a single Chinese national identity, thereby undermining the Tibetan people's fundamental rights, dignity, and national identity. In response to these developments, the Tibetan NGOs and support group jointly issue the following demands to the Chinese government, the United Nations, and the international community: 1. United Nations Response: As Lobga Rangzen made the ultimate sacrifice in front of the United Nations Headquarters, we urge the United Nations to respond in a meaningful and formal manner by addressing the grave human rights situation in Tibet and the circumstances that compelled his sacrifice. 2. Accountability for Tibetans Driven to Self-Immolation: The Chinese government must be held accountable for the policies and repression that have driven Lobga Rangzen and numerous Tibetans to the tragic act of self-immolation. 3. Recognition of Tibet's Sovereignty: Tibet was an independent nation before its occupation by the so called People's Republic of China and remains under Chinese occupation today. We call upon the international community to recognize Tibet's historical status and support the Tibetan people's right to restore their freedom and independence. 4. Repeal the so-called “Ethnic Unity and Progress Law”: We reject this law as an instrument of forced assimilation and call for its immediate repeal and the cessation of its implementation throughout Tibet. 5. International Action and Monitoring: We call upon governments, international organisations, and human rights mechanisms to closely monitor the implementation of the so-called “Ethnic Unity and Progress law”, investigate its impact on Tibetans and other peoples under Chinese rule, and hold the so-called People's Republic of China accountable under international human rights standards. Tenzing Pasang, National Director of Students for a Free Tibet said, "We reject and condemn the recent statement made by Mr Stéphane Dujarric, spokesperson of the Secretary-General (United Nations) referring to Tibet as a "minority." Such characterization is historically inaccurate, politically misleading, and serves only to reinforce the Chinese Communist Party's propaganda. Tibet is not a minority of China. It is an occupied nation with its own distinct history, civilization, language, culture, religion, government, and national identity. Calling Tibet a "minority" erases its national identity and undermines the Tibetan people's right to freedom and independence. "We call on the United Nations to uphold truth and impartiality. It must not use language that legitimizes China's occupation of Tibet or erases the Tibetan nation's identity. The United Nations' words shape global opinion. They must not legitimize occupation or contribute to the erasure of Tibet's identity and the Tibetan people's aspirations for freedom," she concluded. Tibet Self-immolation

title: Tibetan Youth Congress Launches a Global Series of Protests Against PRC - Tibet Post International
content: Dharamshala — Tibetan Youth Congress launchesd a Worldwide Chain Protest in Memory of Martyr Lobga Rangzen and Rejects China's so-called "Ethnic Unity Law" on Sunday. They said," The law provides a legal framework for enforcing political conformity and accelerating the assimilation of peoples living under Chinese occupation and rule, including Tibet, East Turkistan, Southern Mongolia, and Manchuria. Unity cannot be created through coercion." The Tibetan Youth Congress (TYC) launched of a Worldwide Chain Protest in Memory of Martyr Lobga Rangzen and Rejects China's so-called "Ethnic Unity and progressive Law", beginning from Dharamshala on July 19, 2026 and expanding across the globe through our regional chapters and supporters, nearly 20 countries across the world. The first group of people participating in the hunger strike includes Lobsang Tsering, Gonpo Dhondup, Karma Yeshe, Lobsang Yeshe, Tenzin Lhamo, and Penpa Tsering—all former members of the executive committee of the Central Tibetan Youth Congress.The TYC will organise a month-long hunger strike in Dharamsala, after which its members will travel to New Delhi and other locations where the regional TYC existed. Furthermore, the Worldwide Chain Protest in Memory of Martyr Lobga Rangzen and Rejects China's so-called "Ethnic Unity and progressive Law", — will take place in New York and at various locations across the United States, Canada, Europe, and other countries to continue the campaign. Tenzin Lobsang, general secretary of TYC read out the statement of TYC and said, "This international campaign honors the life and final appeal of Tibetan martyr Lobga Rangzen, who died following his self-imolation protest outside of United Nations Headquarters in New York, on July 2, 2026. "Lobga Rangzen devoted his life to the Tibetan freedom movement. His death must not be reduced to a passing tragedy or met only with words of condolence. His final protest was an appeal to the conscience of the international community and a reminder that Tibet remains an occupied nation whose people continue to struggle for freedom and independence. "His appeal cannot be ignored, buried, or erased. The Tibetan Youth Congress will carry his message forward through sustained, collective, and nonviolent action until the Tibetan people's struggle receives the international attention and action it demands. "Beginning in Dharamshala, TYC will organise a chain hunger strike accompanied by coordinated demonstrations, candlelight vigils, public rallies, awareness campaigns, diplomatic outreach, and peaceful direct actions. TYC chapters and supporters worldwide will continue these actions in succession, standing together unity, and resistance." Tashi Dharjee, Vice President of TYC said, "The Tibetan Youth Congress unequivocally rejects the "Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law" imposed by the so-called People's Republic of China. The law, which came into force on July 1, 2026, provides a legal framework for enforcing political conformity and accelerating the assimilation of peoples living under Chinese occupation and rule, including Tibet, East Turkistan, Southern Mongolia, and Manchuria. "Unity cannot be created through coercion. Behind the language of "ethnic unity", this law strengthens a unilateral system through, which the Chinese government suppresses distinct languages, dominates religious institutions, rewrites history, destroys cultural hentage, separates children from their families and communities through state-run colonial boardino schools, and demands absolute loyalty to the Chinese Communist Party. "A government cannot legislate away the identity of a nation. A policy intended to erase a people's language, culture, history, and spiritual heritage is not unity. It is state-enforced assimilation." TYC activists said, "in response to the self-immolation of Martyr Lobga Rangzen, the continuing occupation of Tibet, and the implementation of China's assimilation law, the Tibetan Youth Congress issues the following demands: 1. A formal and substantive response from the United Nations: Lobga Rangzen carried out his final protest outside the United Nations Headquarters. The United Nations must respond with more than condolences. We call upon the Secretary-General, the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, and relevant UN mechanisms to formally address the human rights crisis in Tibet and the circumstances that led to his protest. The United Nations must press China to grant meaningful and unfettered access to Tibet for UN experts, independent observers, and international journalists. 2. An end to language that erases Tibet's national identity: We reject the framing used by Stéphane Dujarric, Spokesperson for the UN Secretary-General, which treated the Tibetan people merely as a "minority" within China. Such language is historically inaccurate and politically consequential. It reinforces the Chinese Communist Party's narrative, erases Tibet's independent national identity, and undermines the Tibetan people's right to freedom and independence. The United Nations must uphold truth and impartiality. Its language must not legitimize China's occupation or prejudge the political status and aspirations of the Tibetan people. 3. Accountability for the repression that has driven Tibetans to self-immolation: The Chinese government must be held accountable for the policies and repression that have created the conditions in which LobgaRangzen and numerous other Tibetans have resorted to the act of self-immolation. We call upon the United Nations and governments worldwide to investigate, document, and publicly challenge China's violations of the political, cultural, linguistic, and religious rights of the Tibetan people. 4. Recognition of Tibet's sovereignty and right to independence: Tibet was an independent nation before its occupation by the People's Republic of China and remains under Chinese occupation today. We call upon goverments, parliaments, and intermational institutions to recognize Tibet's historical status, reject the characterization of Tibet as merely an internal matter of China, and support the Tibetan people's right to restore their freedom and independence. 5. Immediate repeal of the so-called Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law: We reject immediately repeal it, halt its implementation throughout Tibet, and end all policies intended to eliminate Tibet's distinct national, linguistic, cultural, and religious identity. 6. The immediate and unconditional release of all Tibetan political prisoners: We demand the inmediate and unconditional release of the 1l th Panchen Lama, who became the world's youngest political prisoners after being taken into Chinese custody as a child. We further demand the release of all Tibetan political prisoners including environmental activists, artists, writers, religious figures, and others imprisoned for peacefully defending Tibet's land, identity, culture, religion, language, and freedom. Lobga Rangzen's death does not mark the end of his struggle. It is a renewed call for resistance, solidarity, and international action. It confronts the world with a choice: continued silence in the face of occupation and forced assimilation, or meaningful action in defense of truth, freedom, and justice. The United Nations cannot remain a silent witness. Governments cannot continue to treat Tibet as an inconvenient issue to be ignored. Silence enables repression, and inaction allows the destruction of a nation to continue. Lobga Rangzen's courage has become a symbol of the unbreakable Tibetan spirit. We honor Lobga Rangzen's life by amplifying his voice through our movement, our unity, and our unwavering commitment to Tibet's independence." Tibet Free Tibet hunger strike

title: Over 1000 Tibetans cross Europe mark 49th Day of Lobga Rangzen’s self-immolation in Geneva
content: Geneva — More than 1,000 Tibetans and supporters from ten European countries gathered Wednesday in Geneva, to commemorate the 49th day since Lobga Rangzen’s self-immolation in front of the United Nations headquarters in New York and to protest against the Chinese genocidal law being enforced in Tibet. They also called on the international community to defend the rights, identity, and freedom of the Tibetan people. According the office of Tibet, Geneva, the large-scale demonstration and prayer rally began with a march from the Palais Wilson to the United Nations headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland, and concluded near the “broken chair,” a long-standing symbol of the fight against landmines and violence.In the evening, participants gathered at the same location for a candlelight prayer ceremony in remembrance of Lobga Rangzen and his sacrifice. This commemoration brought together more than 1,000 Tibetans from Tibetan communities and organisations in Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Germany, the Netherlands, Spain, France, Austria, Sweden, Italy, and the United Kingdom, alongside the Swiss Association of Tibetan Women, the Gesellschaft Schweizerisch-Tibetische Freundschaft (GSTF), the Tibetan Youth Association in Europe (TYAE), and V-TAG. Leaders from the Tibetan community across Europe also addressed the assembly. The distinguished guests in attendance included Cédric Jeanneret, Member of the Grand Council of Geneva, who attended and addressed the gathering, and Merce, Secretary of UNPO, who also delivered remarks. Thomas Buchli, President of GSTF, read a Statement from the Swiss Parliamentary Group for Tibet. Representatives of the French-speaking Swiss Tibetan Friends group also spoke in solidarity with the Tibetan cause. Representing the Tibet Bureau Geneva, Representative Thinlay Chukki, together with Phuntsok Topgyal, UN Advocacy Officer, and Sangye Kep, EU-China Liaison Officer, attended the demonstration. Representative Thinlay Chukki addressed the gathering and stressed that the commemoration was not only an expression of remembrance, but also a renewed appeal to the international community to act. In her remarks, Representative Thinlay Chukki said that the gathering in front of the United Nations was particularly significant because it marked the 49th day since Lobga Rangzen sacrificed his life in front of the UN Headquarters in New York. “As we assemble today here, we want to commemorate his sacrifice, but also signal to the international community that we have not lost faith and hope yet.” She recalled that Tibetans in exile, under the leadership of His Holiness the Dalai Lama, have consistently spoken for the rights and freedom of Tibetans inside Tibet since 1959. She said Lobga Rangzen’s sacrifice reflected the profound distress caused by policies that, in the Tibetan community’s view, threaten Tibet’s cultural identity, language and heritage. Representative Chukki strongly criticised the Ethnic Unity and Progress Law, saying that its implementation represents a serious threat to Tibetan identity and cultural rights. She expressed concern that the law could further restrict the preservation and use of the Tibetan language and culture and intensify restrictions on those advocating for Tibetan rights. She further warned that provisions targeting organisations and individuals who support Tibetan rights could contribute to transnational repression, extending the impact of restrictive policies beyond Tibet’s borders. “Therefore, I want to say to the United Nations, to the international community and the international organisations, we are here today to not only show a protest against the Chinese law, but also to state that we still have hope that you will stand for Tibetans, for Tibet and for Tibetans inside Tibet,” she said. Addressing the UN human rights mechanisms and governments directly, Representative Chukki urged the UN Special Procedures, the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, ambassadors and governments to move beyond expressions of concern and take meaningful action. “It is no longer okay to be silent. It is time that you stand up and speak and act on the words that you have committed for.” She also called on Tibetans and their supporters not to lose hope, emphasising the importance of unity and sustained international solidarity. The commemoration concluded with prayers and a candlelight ceremony near the Broken Chair, UNO. Participants observed the 49th day in remembrance of Lobga Rangzen, while reaffirming their commitment to peaceful advocacy for Tibet and calling on the international community to stand with Tibetans facing restrictions on their language, culture, religion and identity. A symbolic hair-cutting ceremony was also held during the commemoration, adding a deeply emotional and cultural dimension to the day’s events. The gathering served as a powerful demonstration of solidarity among Tibetans across Europe and their international supporters. Standing before the United Nations, participants renewed their appeal for the UN and governments to uphold universal human rights and to ensure that the voices and rights of Tibetans inside Tibet are neither ignored nor forgotten. The message from Geneva was clear: Lobga Rangzen’s sacrifice must not be forgotten, and the international community must not remain silent in the face of policies that threaten the survival of Tibet’s distinct identity, language and cultural heritage. Free Tibet World Peace Rangzen

title: Tibetans across the world condemn China information blackout in Tibet-Nepal floods
content: Dharamshala — Tibetan environmentalists and activists, along with a man from Kyirong, held a press conference and condemned the information blackout imposed by the Chinese communist government on Kyirong (Gyirong), Tibet. They said,"Glacial landslide in Tibet and Nepal leaves in wake unprecedented devastation to life and property, China's restriction on aid and access makes relief work harder. Tibet is geologically unstable and dangerously vulnerable to global warming, permafrost melt and glacial retreat. In spite of these fragile conditions, China rarely shares environmental impact reports on their infrastructure and hydropower projects in Tibet." The International Tibet Network and Students for a Free Tibet-India held a press conference titled, "Asia’s Water Tower in Crisis: Tibet-Nepal Flash Floods Demand Transparency" at Tibetan Settlement Office, in Mcleod Ganj, Dharamshala, on September 1, 2026. The speakers were Dhondup Wangmo, a research fellow at the Environment and Development Desk of the Tibet Policy Institute (CTA); Dr Lobsang Yangtso, a senior environmental researcher of the International Tibet Network; Gen Jampa Palden, a monk from Kyirong; and Tashi Dhondup, campaigns coordinator for SFT- India; the talk is moderated by Jyotsna George. Tibetan community members and environmental researchers shared their anguish over the challenges in accessing verified updated information on impact of glacial avalanche that struck Kyirong, Tibet and Rasuwa district of Nepal on August 26, 2026 and said that Nepal and India China should hold accountable for the devastating floods. The Tibet rights groups also called for China to allow international media unfettered access to verify and report on the loss of life and damage in Kyirong, Tibet. It may left estimated 300 homes destroyed in Kyirong and borders of Tibet-Nepal. According the groups, in Tibet, the Chinese state media has reported 16 deaths and more than 558 missing people. In Nepal, official government sources state at least 939 people have lost their lives and over 3925 are still missing, including hundreds of foreign nationals from more than 36 countries. Reports suggest that China has been censoring footage of the glacial floods from Tibet, and some international media houses have reported they have been denied permission to visit Kyirong and independently report on the scale of devastation there. "China exercises iron-fist control on media and information in Tibet, it maintains stability in the occupied territory by imposing a series of restrictions on transmission of information, political and civil liberties, and right of movement for Tibetans. In fact, global civil and political liberties watch-dog Freedom House has consistently ranked Tibet as one the very least free places in the world," the groups said. Jampa Palden, a Buddhist monk from Kyirong, Tibet: "Tibetans inside Tibet face heavy surveillance and censorship. They are not free to share information or updates either on their social media or with their families outside Tibet. These restrictions have been the key reason why no photographic or video evidence of the damage inside Tibet has emerged. Tibetans outside Tibet have no reliable way to learn how many of our fellow Tibetans have been killed, or the true status of relief efforts." Dhondup Wangmo, Research Fellow, Tibet Policy Institute: "This unfortunate disaster underscores what Tibetans have been saying for decades - Tibet is geologically unstable and dangerously vulnerable to global warming, permafrost melt and glacial retreat [7]. In spite of these fragile conditions, China rarely shares environmental impact reports on their infrastructure and hydropower projects in Tibet [8]. Most recently, Chinese geologists and environmentalists have sounded the alarm about the Medog dam, intended to carry three times the capacity of the Three Gorges Dam [9]. Further, all of Asia's major rivers originate in Tibet, feeding nearly 2 billion people downstream [10]. China has a moral responsibility to share transparent data on their ongoing projects, and during disasters, they must proactively share early warnings." Dr Lobsang Yangtso, Senior Researcher, International Tibet Network: "The vulnerability in which Tibetans and the people of Nepal now find themselves is especially cruel, because we have been among the loudest voices warning of both the climate crisis and geological risk. Like the Nepalese communities, Tibetans are among the least contributors to global greenhouse gas emissions [11], yet their location in the Himalayas makes them far more susceptible to climate danger than people in wealthier nations whose emissions are disproportionately high to their population. The Tibetan plateau is warming three times faster than the global average [12]- yet Tibet is rarely mentioned at the COP Climate Summits, and Tibetan climate experts are rarely given a seat at the table." Tashi Dhondup, Campaign Coordinator, Students for a Free Tibet- India: "Under Chinese rule, Tibetans have no freedom to decide how our land is used. We are not consulted when Chinese companies build dams, dig mines, or harness our rivers and extract the rare minerals under our soil. Peaceful protests, like those against the Kamtok dam are met with overwhelming force [13]. Our way of life is systematically eradicated as nomads in their millions are driven from their pastures and pushed into menial jobs [14]. Tibetan lives are dispensable to China, as is evident in their lack of rigorous reporting of loss to Tibetan life and homes in Kyirong county." The environmentalists and activists said, "in August 2024, Tibetans around the world called for a moratorium on extraction and mega-development projects. They announced that so long as Tibet remains occupied and its landscape and natural resources remain under China's control, no further projects, be they mines or dams, should proceed, and that any international companies or investors involved in Tibet should withdraw. This moratorium is more urgent than ever." "Finally, we call on the international community - governments and media organisations in particular - to use Tibetan place names in any statements or reporting, both as a matter of historical accuracy and respect for Tibetan cultural identity. This includes, for example, using Kyidrong instead of the Chinese name 'Gyirong', and Tibet instead of the Chinese name 'Xizang'," they said. Tibetan groups put forward the following four demands: •China must allow international access and assistance to those affected by the flash floods, without interference or obstruction in Tibet • Beijing must not punish Tibetans who share information or attempt to contact family and friends about the impact of the flash floods or its response. • As climate cascading dangers intensify, China must also share timely and accurate early transboundary hydrological data with immediate downstream countries Nepal, India and Bangladesh and provide early warning to them. • International actors, including governments, media organisations and disaster agencies and monitors, must use Tibetan place names at all times in statements and reporting as a matter of basic accuracy, and avoid the use of the Chinese-imposed term "Xizang" which is rejected by Tibetans. Tibet Justice flood Kyirong

title: Tibetan monk remains in critical condition after being tortured by Chinese authorities
content: Dharamshala — A Tibetan monk has been bedridden for two years, unable to stand or speak, and is being fed through a feeding tube, after suffering torture and abuse at the hands of Chinese authorities while in Chinese detention. He had been arrested by the authorities for opposing China’s construction of the Kamtok (Gangtuo) hydroelectric dam, which threatened to destroy centuries-old monasteries in Gege County, Kham, in eastern Tibet. Gonpo Tsering, Tibetan monk and the head of Yena Monastery in Shiba Village, was among the more than 100 Tibetan monks from the Wonto and Yena monasteries who were arrested by Chinese armed forces on February 22, 2024. Many of them were beaten and injured and were subsequently admitted to Dege County Hospital for treatment. Following Gonpo Tsering’s arrest, Chinese authorities subjected him to severe physical abuse and torture while in custody. As a result, he was urgently transported to West China (Huaxi) Hospital in Chengdu, where he has been in critical condition for the past two years. "Gonpo Tsering is currently bedridden, unable to stand or speak, and is fed through tubes. He is unresponsive to family members and unable to recognize people around him. Devastated by his son’s detention and condition, his father, Lobsang Dorjee, passed away on Sep. 21, 2025," the source told ICT. Around 300 Tibetans gathered in front of the Dege county government building on February 14, 2024, and protested against the construction of the largest hydroelectric power plant in their region and the forced displacement of their homes and monasteries. They called on the county authorities to cancel the plan to build the power station and the order to move their homes and monasteries. The Chinese authorities plan to build a 2,240 megawatt hydropower station on the Drichu River (Jinsha River in Chinese) without the Tibetans' consent to dam construction and resettlement, and have ordered Tibetans and monks from six monasteries and two villages in two townships of Dege County, Kham, eastern Tibet, to resettle in other villages. Therefore, hundreds of Tibetans gathered in front of the Dege county government building on February 14, 2024 and protested against this action and to ask the concerned authorities to put an end to it. The Chinese authorities brought a specially trained police force to the Wonto village area on February 22, 2024 and arrested more than 100 Tibetan monks from the Wonto and Yena monasteries, as well as local residents, many of whom were beaten and injured before being admitted to Dege County Hospital for treatment. After peaceful protests by Tibetans and Tibetan monks continued from 14 to 22 February, 2024, the Chinese government sent in trained special forces to arrest the demonstrators. Tibetans working outside their villages returned home and asked the Chinese police to release the detained Tibetans. Unfortunately, the Chinese police arrested those who had made this request and detained more than 1,000 Tibetans on February 23, 2024, including Tibetan monks, local Tibetans and Tibetans from outside the villages. The police have asked family members to bring Tsampa-Tibetan food and blankets to the detention centres, as they do not have enough food for large numbers of detainees. Tibetans around the world, from the United States to Canada, Europe and India, have protested against the Chinese government's beating and arrest of Tibetans in Dege, Kham,Tibet, for their peaceful protest against the construction of a mega-dam and for forcibly ordering the relocation of six Tibetan monasteries and two villages in Dege County. Tibetans in exile expressed their deep concern about the unfair treatment of detained Tibetans. They also expressed their solidarity with Tibetans detained in Chinese-occupied Tibet. China-Tibet: The one-thing you need to know Over the past 70 decades, there has been ongoing political repression, social discrimination, economic marginalization, environmental destruction, and cultural assimilation, particularly due to Chinese migration to Tibet which is fueling intense resentment among the people of occupied Tibet. The communist-totalitarian state of China began its invasion of Tibet in 1949, reaching complete occupation of the country in 1959. Since that time, more than 1.2 million people, 20% of the nation's population of six million, have died as a direct result of China's invasion and occupation. In addition, over 99% of Tibet's six thousand religious monasteries, temples, and shrines, have been looted or decimated resulting in the destruction of hundreds of thousands of sacred Buddhist scriptures. Until 1949, Tibet was an independent Buddhist nation in the Himalayas which had little contact with the rest of the world. It existed as a rich cultural storehouse of the Mahayana and Vajrayana teachings of Buddhism. Religion was a unifying theme among the Tibetans -- as was their own language, literature, art, and world view developed by living at high altitudes, under harsh conditions, in a balance with their environment. Tibet Freedom Religion

title: Tibetans call on Switzerland and UN to hold China accountable for its human rights violations in Tibet
content: Bern, Switzerland — More than 200 Tibetans and supporters gathered near the Swiss Parliament in Bern on Friday and held a peaceful demonstration protesting China’s increasingly intense assimilation policies in Tibet, including the “Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress.” The rally also marked the 44th day since Tibetan martyr Lhoba Langzan died by self-immolation; his sacrifice has once again drawn international attention to the human rights situation in Tibet. They called on Switzerland government and the UN to hold China accountable for its human rights violations in Tibet. According to the Office of Tibet, Geneva, the demonstration was organised by the Tibetan Community in Switzerland and Liechtenstein, the Swiss Tibetan Friendship Association (GSTF), the Swiss Tibetan Women’s Association, the European Tibetan Youth Association, and Swiss V-TAG. More than 200 Tibetans and supporters gathered near the Swiss Parliament in Bern on August 14, 2026, for the peaceful demonstration. Among the participants were leaders of the Tibetan community, former Tibetan parliamentarians, former representatives of the Tibet Office, as well as representatives of the Tibet Office in Geneva, including Thinlay Chukki, representative of His Holiness the Dalai Lama, and Phuntsok Topgyal, UN Advocacy Officer. The gathering featured a series of solidarity activities, including the chanting of slogans, a scarf-presentation ceremony in front of a portrait of Pawo Lobga Rangzen, the singing of the Tibetan national anthem, a one-minute silence in memory of Tibetan martyrs, and prayers for peace.
